day long excursion to Sandy hook. targets were Whimbrel, American golden plover, and Philadelphia vireo.  not a huge day for passerines. overcast, except for around 2-4. hot then.  tide was still quite hi when I arrived at 12pm. spermcetti cove had black bellied plovers, SEPL, RUTU, but all distant.  explored north end mudflats next where tide was starting to recede. very few shorebirds but immense tern colony. sure to have been roseates mixed in with common but couldn't pick any out.  stayed until around 4pm, then walked the beach south down to the North Beach parking lot. eider was just offshore there, a long with a few piping plovers.  made another pass at sperm cove, this time with much of the mudflats exposed. more AMOY and BBPL now but no good American golden candidates.  went back to North end mudflats right around 530 and found two Whimbrel sitting right in the main leftover puddle on the flats. took most of my photos there and then watched them takeoff. they then flew back in, this time with 4 more, and did several aerial passes of the flats doing flight calls. pretty spectacular to watch. briefly touched down nearby for a few more photos and then left the area just before sunset.  successful and movie-esque day!

all morning search for Ms. wandering tattler  success in the final hour right before island packer.  More details:  Started at the jetty across from Island Packer lot. Wasn't having a ton of luck there, so drove to the other side of the creek mouth to scope from there, where I got absolutely nailed by a wave. Had to go to CVS to get lens cleaner to clean my scope, nocs, and glasses. Came back to the north side and continued scoping from safer locations away from waves. Still no luck with Tattler. Drove back to the south side of the creek mouth and checked the "surfers knoll" area, then back to the initial scoping spot across from Island Packers. There was a surfing competition going on, and one of the announcements was loud enough to scare up a flock of shorebirds previously tucked away in the rocky jetty. Out of this mostly white-wing striped crowd (willet, surfbird, turnstone, peep), there was one all dark-winged individual that I immediately clocked and stayed on with nocs. It flew across the beach in front of me and landed on the north shoreline, a little before the start of the jetty. I checked my sibley app and found that indeed the tattler had all dark wings, so sprinted up the beach with my scope and found the tattler blended in perfectly with the rocks. Was an awesome chase day with a skin-of-my-teeth rewarding ending as I had to go check in with the Island Packers boat 15 minutes later.

11:20-1ish stationary skywatch by her majesty  then a loop of the park  chatted with madeleine.  sick day can't stop me from getting two new park birds and one Bronx bird    so rip to birdcast: it officially turned off on november 15 and we wont be graced with her presence again until March 1.  seemed like an overall big migration night though with many bluebirds, pipits, and songbirds reported all over the city.  initial plan was to celebrate being done with work by waking up at sunrise and doing morning flight at franz, then drive to pelham to meet up with rich and alyssa. but a fever intervened and i spent the night shivering, falling asleep at 4 and finally waking up at 1030 to a lot of FOMO from reports all over the city of big bird movement.    felt marginally better though, so i bundled up, got a smoothie and a sandwich and plopped down in the grass on the watch hill for a stationary 1:30 min watch.  enormously successful with one flyover pipit (picked up by merlin and then me moments later). wish i had gotten eyes on him because he sounded VERY close. would've loved a pic. N to S flight.  alyssa then posted a bluebird at pelham and i got very salty because my cold thwarted my target bird bluebird plans. it didn't help that merlin told me bluebird was my bird of the day.  but literally as i was sending her a screenshot of my BotD and complaining that i'd never see one at franz, a tuwuwuwU call came out of the sky to the W of me. i glanced down at merlin and it agreed with me: tuwuwuWU for sure.  incredibly, i got eyes and photos on a flock of 8 of them as they flew north over the NW woods of the park.  pretty quiet after that excitement. i thought bluebird was a county bird for me, but it turns out i saw one last year at pelham (where i also met hailey for the first time). but still a franz bird is just as good.    this songbird flight gave way to a slow but steady movement of raptors. many TUVU, red tailed hawks, and a bunch of extremely high up buteos I couldn't make out. I was also watching the CT group me where there were more reports of Golden Eagles drifting towards NY.    black vulture, broad winged hawk, bald eagle, golden eagle, and red-shouldered hawk were all the targets as my brain switched to raptor mode.    and lo and behold, a red-shouldered came over with a sharpie and a RTHA. beautiful orange underneath with black and white fringing to the wings and a lovely banded tail. i was worried i wouldn't recognize one if it came by, so i took a ton of pics just to be sure, but my instincts were right.    overall an amazing outcome for a late start day. welcome new franz birds 128 and 129: eastern bluebird and red-shouldered hawk <3

day long excursion to Sandy hook. targets were Whimbrel, American golden plover, and Philadelphia vireo.  not a huge day for passerines. overcast, except for around 2-4. hot then.  tide was still quite hi when I arrived at 12pm. spermcetti cove had black bellied plovers, SEPL, RUTU, but all distant.  explored north end mudflats next where tide was starting to recede. very few shorebirds but immense tern colony. sure to have been roseates mixed in with common but couldn't pick any out.  stayed until around 4pm, then walked the beach south down to the North Beach parking lot. eider was just offshore there, a long with a few piping plovers.  made another pass at sperm cove, this time with much of the mudflats exposed. more AMOY and BBPL now but no good American golden candidates.  went back to North end mudflats right around 530 and found two Whimbrel sitting right in the main leftover puddle on the flats. took most of my photos there and then watched them takeoff. they then flew back in, this time with 4 more, and did several aerial passes of the flats doing flight calls. pretty spectacular to watch. briefly touched down nearby for a few more photos and then left the area just before sunset.  successful and movie-esque day!

Checklist Comments: Arrived still in the dark to see one birder, Matt, already with his scope up. Did a few NYtimes games on my phone until it got slightly more reasonable of lighting conditions and joined him. Gorgeous view from up above the berm. Tons of dark shadow sleeping geese -- estimated at least a thousand by best guess.  Then the Where's Waldo game began as more light gave us more details on the birds. Over half were still sleeping. Scanned through the ones in the water many times as it would be most obvious there, but remained pretty sure it wasn't among them. Several trips to the car to refill coffee and add more layers of clothing, and the several more birders joined us.  At approximately 720ish, I caught a glimpse of white fringing on some wing feathers of a sleeping goose tucked in. I called it out and got everyone on it. Despite being almost entirely certain this HAD to be our tundra goose, I didn't want to post it to the Rhode Island groupme until it's head came untucked. And low and behold around 730, it did. I sent the alert out, the whole crew congratulated each other, and I believe Matt got back home in time for baseball.  Great to meet Danny and Ron. Super fun morning of sitting and watching the goose walk around, preen, swim, drink water, and take multiple naps.  Later in the morning I joined others closer down on the reservoir-edge berm. We watched it cozy up into a flock of sleeping canadas, and then I took my eyes off it for a moment, heard a commotion of a few geese flying, and completely lost it. it must've taken off right as I took my eyes off. Amazing bird and great way to celebrate the end of January recitals

Possible manx candidate seen twice throughout the day as well, but not good enough looks to confirm. tons of gannet early on as well.    edit: not seeing a place to put a possible jaeger sp. but i want to record my notes before i forget them: very white bellied bird with dark cutoff at rear and front (forming an almost square white belly impression). dark underwings with white patches in the middle. head not giving "Capped" appearance, but instead a dark overall face. wings long feeling and held up and arched in a gannet-like way, but not a gannet's head. odd bird.

day long excursion to Sandy hook. targets were Whimbrel, American golden plover, and Philadelphia vireo.  not a huge day for passerines. overcast, except for around 2-4. hot then.  tide was still quite hi when I arrived at 12pm. spermcetti cove had black bellied plovers, SEPL, RUTU, but all distant.  explored north end mudflats next where tide was starting to recede. very few shorebirds but immense tern colony. sure to have been roseates mixed in with common but couldn't pick any out.  stayed until around 4pm, then walked the beach south down to the North Beach parking lot. eider was just offshore there, a long with a few piping plovers.  made another pass at sperm cove, this time with much of the mudflats exposed. more AMOY and BBPL now but no good American golden candidates.  went back to North end mudflats right around 530 and found two Whimbrel sitting right in the main leftover puddle on the flats. took most of my photos there and then watched them takeoff. they then flew back in, this time with 4 more, and did several aerial passes of the flats doing flight calls. pretty spectacular to watch. briefly touched down nearby for a few more photos and then left the area just before sunset.  successful and movie-esque day!

dope shearwater morning.  started off solo at about 6am and soon joined by brian. began at lookout from restaurant, then at the lookout just southeast with the bluff on our right, then out at the rock slabs in front of the lighthouse. brief peek around the parking lot/restroom area afterwards. lots of shearwater activity. picked out the target sooty shearwater soon after brian arrived. possible jaeger moving east to west early before brian's arrival, then another while still at the restaurant. Not confident or good enough looks to count it. Possible manx candidate seen twice throughout the day as well, but not good enough looks to confirm. tons of gannet early on as well.    edit: not seeing a place to put a possible jaeger sp. but i want to record my notes before i forget them: very white bellied bird with dark cutoff at rear and front (forming an almost square white belly impression). dark underwings with white patches in the middle. head not giving "Capped" appearance, but instead a dark overall face. wings long feeling and held up and arched in a gannet-like way, but not a gannet's head. odd bird.

day long excursion to Sandy hook. targets were Whimbrel, American golden plover, and Philadelphia vireo.  not a huge day for passerines. overcast, except for around 2-4. hot then.  tide was still quite hi when I arrived at 12pm. spermcetti cove had black bellied plovers, SEPL, RUTU, but all distant.  explored north end mudflats next where tide was starting to recede. very few shorebirds but immense tern colony. sure to have been roseates mixed in with common but couldn't pick any out.  stayed until around 4pm, then walked the beach south down to the North Beach parking lot. eider was just offshore there, a long with a few piping plovers.  made another pass at sperm cove, this time with much of the mudflats exposed. more AMOY and BBPL now but no good American golden candidates.  went back to North end mudflats right around 530 and found two Whimbrel sitting right in the main leftover puddle on the flats. took most of my photos there and then watched them takeoff. they then flew back in, this time with 4 more, and did several aerial passes of the flats doing flight calls. pretty spectacular to watch. briefly touched down nearby for a few more photos and then left the area just before sunset.  successful and movie-esque day!

Location: Oregon Inlet Pelagic -- On the Shelf (Inshore of the Shelf Break)
Checklist Comments: Seabirding pelagic trip aboard the Stormy Petrel II, from Oregon Inlet offshore to the shelf break. We headed a bit more to the east today and worked the shelf break a bit so we have five lists for today. On the shelf to the break, offshore of the break, back on the shelf for a bit then offshore again ending with the usual inshore tack toward the inlet. Location: Oregon Inlet Pelagic -- On the Shelf (Inshore of the Shelf Break)
Checklist Comments: Seabirding pelagic trip aboard the Stormy Petrel II, from the shelf break inshore for a bit to see what we could find. There were definitely more Wilson's in here than offshore, so we worked some temperature breaks for a bit. Winds were about 10 from the north and skies partly cloudy for this leg. There were some sharks leaping out of the water and spinning ahead and as we approached their location those in the bow were able to look down and see over 100 swimming below the surface! It looks like these were possibly Spinner Sharks, but also could have been Black-tipped Sharks.

day long excursion to Sandy hook. targets were Whimbrel, American golden plover, and Philadelphia vireo.  not a huge day for passerines. overcast, except for around 2-4. hot then.  tide was still quite hi when I arrived at 12pm. spermcetti cove had black bellied plovers, SEPL, RUTU, but all distant.  explored north end mudflats next where tide was starting to recede. very few shorebirds but immense tern colony. sure to have been roseates mixed in with common but couldn't pick any out.  stayed until around 4pm, then walked the beach south down to the North Beach parking lot. eider was just offshore there, a long with a few piping plovers.  made another pass at sperm cove, this time with much of the mudflats exposed. more AMOY and BBPL now but no good American golden candidates.  went back to North end mudflats right around 530 and found two Whimbrel sitting right in the main leftover puddle on the flats. took most of my photos there and then watched them takeoff. they then flew back in, this time with 4 more, and did several aerial passes of the flats doing flight calls. pretty spectacular to watch. briefly touched down nearby for a few more photos and then left the area just before sunset.  successful and movie-esque day!

since i had missed my Vaux's Swift at bear divide earlier, i checked ebird for recent reports that were on the way from bear divide to ballona creek where i had to get that afternoon. Michael Klotz and Carli Wyllie had reported some at "Sepulveda Basin--East of Woodley Ave" on 4/16, so that became the next stop. Eyeballing the map, I thought the east basin close to the 405 would be the most likely spot, so I tried there first. TONS of swallows on the water, which I tried to photograph for quite awhile hoping to land a swift. But they were all foraging right on the water, whereas my gut was telling me a swift would prefer to be foraging high up in the air. After not turning up anything for about 30 minutes, I checked ebird once again and saw that a new report from Robert Thoren had just come in on 4/17 that there were two at the Lake Balboa hotspot on the other side of the park. I hightailed it over there, jumped out of the car and saw a MASSIVE flock of swallows circling above the parking lot. This seemed WAY more promising, as they were all up high. I ditched the camera for awhile and just stared up at different shapes, trying to remember what Matt told me last year when we were looking for a white throated swift when I asked him how he was able to tell apart a swift from a swallow: "swifts just look like swifts--not like swallows."  And boom. Something that looked like a swift. Smaller, no real protruding tail feathers, and all dark. Tracked it for awhile in bins and then switched to camera and got some idable shots. Great last lifer for the trip

all morning search for Ms. wandering tattler  success in the final hour right before island packer.  More details:  Started at the jetty across from Island Packer lot. Wasn't having a ton of luck there, so drove to the other side of the creek mouth to scope from there, where I got absolutely nailed by a wave. Had to go to CVS to get lens cleaner to clean my scope, nocs, and glasses. Came back to the north side and continued scoping from safer locations away from waves. Still no luck with Tattler. Drove back to the south side of the creek mouth and checked the "surfers knoll" area, then back to the initial scoping spot across from Island Packers. There was a surfing competition going on, and one of the announcements was loud enough to scare up a flock of shorebirds previously tucked away in the rocky jetty. Out of this mostly white-wing striped crowd (willet, surfbird, turnstone, peep), there was one all dark-winged individual that I immediately clocked and stayed on with nocs. It flew across the beach in front of me and landed on the north shoreline, a little before the start of the jetty. I checked my sibley app and found that indeed the tattler had all dark wings, so sprinted up the beach with my scope and found the tattler blended in perfectly with the rocks. Was an awesome chase day with a skin-of-my-teeth rewarding ending as I had to go check in with the Island Packers boat 15 minutes later.

Checklist Comments: all morning search for Ms. wandering tattler  success in the final hour right before island packer.  More details:  Started at the jetty across from Island Packer lot. Wasn't having a ton of luck there, so drove to the other side of the creek mouth to scope from there, where I got absolutely nailed by a wave. Had to go to CVS to get lens cleaner to clean my scope, nocs, and glasses. Came back to the north side and continued scoping from safer locations away from waves. Still no luck with Tattler. Drove back to the south side of the creek mouth and checked the "surfers knoll" area, then back to the initial scoping spot across from Island Packers. There was a surfing competition going on, and one of the announcements was loud enough to scare up a flock of shorebirds previously tucked away in the rocky jetty. Out of this mostly white-wing striped crowd (willet, surfbird, turnstone, peep), there was one all dark-winged individual that I immediately clocked and stayed on with nocs. It flew across the beach in front of me and landed on the north shoreline, a little before the start of the jetty. I checked my sibley app and found that indeed the tattler had all dark wings, so sprinted up the beach with my scope and found the tattler blended in perfectly with the rocks. Was an awesome chase day with a skin-of-my-teeth rewarding ending as I had to go check in with the Island Packers boat 15 minutes later.

Checklist Comments: bonkers day of cave swallow watching at the southern zone landfill. joined early on by rich aracil, then later by Alyssa Bueno. Pat also made a brief appearance.  started on the shore just south of the sparrow landfill fence. later moved south to the first beachy peninsula, then found a sweet spot in the middle of those two on the rocky shore near the big graffiti rock. this seemed to be perfectly in line with the consistent swallow flight path.  they continually appeared cresting over the eastern hills of the landfill and making a more or less direct flight across the water over towards us. theoretically it would line up in a pretty direct line with turtle cove and the lagoon at Pelham. would make sense that they are coming down the coast and then hug the lagoon side once hunter island splits off.  super exciting long bird day and memorable as heck.

Location: Oregon Inlet Pelagic -- Offshore / Gulf Stream
Checklist Comments: Seabirding pelagic trip aboard the Stormy Petrel II, from the shelf offshore to about 800 fathoms (5,600 feet) and back inshore to the shelf break. Skies cleared during this period and winds were still about 11 mph from the northwest, falling out and shifting to the north northwest. During this period we also saw on large, unidentified whale, at least 24 to 28 Offshore Bottlenose Dolphins, about 17 Pilot Whales (prob. short finned), one Ocean Sunfish (Mola mola), one Sailfish, and one Mako Shark.

Location: Oregon Inlet Pelagic -- Offshore / Gulf Stream
Checklist Comments: Seabirding pelagic trip aboard the Stormy Petrel II, from the shelf break offshore to about 600 fathoms (3,600 feet) and back to the shelf break. Winds were from the north west then north northwest at about 7 to 12 mph and skies were partly cloudy. We also saw 22 Pilot Whales (likely Short-finned) and 50 to 75 Offshore Bottlenose Dolphins on this leg. There was not much bird life out there in the deeper water, so we headed back toward the shelf to see if we could find some life in there...thus this list is a bit shorter than usual.

Location: Oregon Inlet Pelagic -- Offshore / Gulf Stream
Checklist Comments: Seabirding pelagic trip aboard the Stormy Petrel II, from the shelf break offshore to about 300 or 350 fathoms (1800 to 2100 feet) and back to the shelf break. Winds fell back out to 7 to 9 mph during this leg from the north east. Again, we didn't find much bird life offshore of the shelf so we tacked back in, but we did catch and release a White Marlin, see 7 Ocean Sunfish (Mola mola) swimming together near a Sargassum line, and had at least four Scalloped / Carolina Hammerheads swim by the boat!

Location: Oregon Inlet Pelagic -- On the Shelf (Inshore of the Shelf Break)
Checklist Comments: Seabirding pelagic trip aboard the Stormy Petrel II, from Oregon Inlet offshore to the shelf break. It was overcast for most of this leg and winds were about 11 mph from the northwest. We saw a couple pods of Atlantic Spotted Dolphins totaling about 17 to 20 individuals on this leg.

Location: Oregon Inlet Pelagic -- On the Shelf (Inshore of the Shelf Break)
Checklist Comments: Seabirding pelagic trip aboard the Stormy Petrel II, from the shelf break back inshore to Oregon Inlet. Winds fell out to less than 5 mph on this leg and skies were cloudy. We also saw a pod of about 40 or 50 Atlantic Spotted Dolphins, two Leatherback Turtles, one Ocean Sunfish (Mola mola), and one shark species.

Location: Oregon Inlet Pelagic -- On the Shelf (Inshore of the Shelf Break)
Checklist Comments: Seabirding pelagic trip aboard the Stormy Petrel II, from Oregon Inlet offshore to the shelf break. We headed a bit more to the east today and worked the shelf break a bit so we have five lists for today. On the shelf to the break, offshore of the break, back on the shelf for a bit then offshore again ending with the usual inshore tack toward the inlet. Skies were partly cloudy this morning and the winds were from the north west at about 5 mph. We saw about 20 Pilot Whales (likely Short-finned) and caught a Wahoo on this leg.

Location: Oregon Inlet Pelagic -- On the Shelf (Inshore of the Shelf Break)
Checklist Comments: Seabirding pelagic trip aboard the Stormy Petrel II, from the shelf break inshore for a bit to see what we could find. There were definitely more Wilson's in here than offshore, so we worked some temperature breaks for a bit. Winds were about 10 from the north and skies partly cloudy for this leg. There were some sharks leaping out of the water and spinning ahead and as we approached their location those in the bow were able to look down and see over 100 swimming below the surface! It looks like these were possibly Spinner Sharks, but also could have been Black-tipped Sharks.

Location: Oregon Inlet Pelagic -- On the Shelf (Inshore of the Shelf Break)
Checklist Comments: Seabirding pelagic trip aboard the Stormy Petrel II, from the shelf break back inshore to Oregon Inlet. It breezed up a bit from the north for our trip back to the inlet, but before we picked up we got to check a nice Sargassum line that had some life on it. This feature was just inshore of the shelf break. We also had at least 21 Offshore Bottlenose Dolphins on this leg.

Checklist Comments: dope shearwater morning.  started off solo at about 6am and soon joined by brian. began at lookout from restaurant, then at the lookout just southeast with the bluff on our right, then out at the rock slabs in front of the lighthouse. brief peek around the parking lot/restroom area afterwards. lots of shearwater activity. picked out the target sooty shearwater soon after brian arrived. possible jaeger moving east to west early before brian's arrival, then another while still at the restaurant. Not confident or good enough looks to count it. Possible manx candidate seen twice throughout the day as well, but not good enough looks to confirm. tons of gannet early on as well.    edit: not seeing a place to put a possible jaeger sp. but i want to record my notes before i forget them: very white bellied bird with dark cutoff at rear and front (forming an almost square white belly impression). dark underwings with white patches in the middle. head not giving "Capped" appearance, but instead a dark overall face. wings long feeling and held up and arched in a gannet-like way, but not a gannet's head. odd bird.

Observation Details: 1 scopoli's that flew close to shore that i never would've ID'd called out by Peter. he has pics. i MAY have pics but have to go through them all. very white underwing extending out to primaries.  Haha turns out i have at least one blurry pic that is taken at the same instant as one from Peter's confirmed checklist. see the right wing halfway dipped in water with the fish in its mouth. A much better pic: https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/625449083  wild and unexpected lifer--i was thinking maybe i'd luck into a few underwing shots and could study up but it was so nice to have an expert there to call out when it was flying past. Been going through photos for the last two days and I'm pretty sure I can tell the difference now between Cory's and the Scop. If I've labeled some of these wrong, please let me know! I'm especially curious about the 2 photos i have with two birds flying next to each other -- these were taken milliseconds apart and i believe show a cory on the right and scop on the left. Lifer and 478!

first big target bird of the trip.  parked at the airboat tour parking lot and began by checking the massive tree full of fish crow and grackles above the ramp. no cowbirds. walked north up the street and saw a few more grackle in between the houses. walked back south on the other side and got side tracked by egrets and herons.  then did a walk out to the west most road and saw my first female BH cowbird. seemed like a promising sign.  walked south from the airboat lot and found a tree with at least 6 roosting cowbirds in it. did a careful check of each but all had dark eyes and similar shape/beak shape. there were a lot of tangled nooks and crannies though, so I felt like it was possible I had missed some. chatted with a local and then walked back up to the parking area to check the big boat ramp tree. still no cowbirds.  walked BACK out to the west most road and found another small roost of cowbirds and grackles. most of the brown headed were all perched and not moving, but one was jumping from branch to branch and caught my eye. got enough of a peak at the face to see something was different with its eye. immediately grabbed camera and snapped some pics to reveal a red iris with a black pupil suspended in the middle.  glorious feeling. called Matt to tell him about it.  took a few more pics and then dipped cuz I thought everyone was probably sick of me walking through their neighborhood.  fun first lifer :)

Observation Details: continuing NYC celeb. shocking when you walk up to it for the first time. actually feels like a Jim Henson puppet. or a real life dinosaur. black on tail and wings, otherwise white feathers. patchy psoriasis-like facial skin. fuzzy peach head and neck.  watched it for about an hour and saw several behaviors:  sunning itself, wings held slightly away from body, almost looking like a kid in a ghost sheet costume for Halloween. defecated three times and was shocked at how unlike other birds it was: more of a one or two second stream than a typical spritz. preening feathers constantly, and vocalizing quietly with still strong nasal "henks."  quiet bill snaps every once in awhile after preening.  lifer and year #471  crazy experience 10/10 almost worth the SIR

all morning search for Ms. wandering tattler  success in the final hour right before island packer.  More details:  Started at the jetty across from Island Packer lot. Wasn't having a ton of luck there, so drove to the other side of the creek mouth to scope from there, where I got absolutely nailed by a wave. Had to go to CVS to get lens cleaner to clean my scope, nocs, and glasses. Came back to the north side and continued scoping from safer locations away from waves. Still no luck with Tattler. Drove back to the south side of the creek mouth and checked the "surfers knoll" area, then back to the initial scoping spot across from Island Packers. There was a surfing competition going on, and one of the announcements was loud enough to scare up a flock of shorebirds previously tucked away in the rocky jetty. Out of this mostly white-wing striped crowd (willet, surfbird, turnstone, peep), there was one all dark-winged individual that I immediately clocked and stayed on with nocs. It flew across the beach in front of me and landed on the north shoreline, a little before the start of the jetty. I checked my sibley app and found that indeed the tattler had all dark wings, so sprinted up the beach with my scope and found the tattler blended in perfectly with the rocks. Was an awesome chase day with a skin-of-my-teeth rewarding ending as I had to go check in with the Island Packers boat 15 minutes later.

absolutely stellar morning at Franz.  started at my usual spot mid park where it was a bit quiet and dark still. but heard what sounded like a great crested coming from the ball fields to the south. realized I never really check the tree line from INSIDE the ball fields, and have seen people running their dogs in there, so went to go check it out.  best decision of the day. immediately started hearing tons of warbler song, and the sun was hitting these southwest trees in full getting the bugs really active.  btgreen, mag, BTblue, yellow, and redstart were all quite readily found, a long with a vocal RBGR  biggest shocker came with a Wilson's warbler tucked deep in the lower branches. my first for the Bronx and a first of the year for me. huge win.  swallows came next with a glance at a tree swallow and good looks at a barn swallow.  hung around for an hour or so before exploring the rest of the park, which yielded some really close views of feeding Blackpolls in a reddish purple beech tree (thanks Jules)  gb heron flyover really cinched the morning.  wanted ovenbird and a thrush on the way out, so walked the Walton slopes and got my patch Swainsons :)))  most fire morning of the Franz season

since i had missed my Vaux's Swift at bear divide earlier, i checked ebird for recent reports that were on the way from bear divide to ballona creek where i had to get that afternoon. Michael Klotz and Carli Wyllie had reported some at "Sepulveda Basin--East of Woodley Ave" on 4/16, so that became the next stop. Eyeballing the map, I thought the east basin close to the 405 would be the most likely spot, so I tried there first. TONS of swallows on the water, which I tried to photograph for quite awhile hoping to land a swift. But they were all foraging right on the water, whereas my gut was telling me a swift would prefer to be foraging high up in the air. After not turning up anything for about 30 minutes, I checked ebird once again and saw that a new report from Robert Thoren had just come in on 4/17 that there were two at the Lake Balboa hotspot on the other side of the park. I hightailed it over there, jumped out of the car and saw a MASSIVE flock of swallows circling above the parking lot. This seemed WAY more promising, as they were all up high. I ditched the camera for awhile and just stared up at different shapes, trying to remember what Matt told me last year when we were looking for a white throated swift when I asked him how he was able to tell apart a swift from a swallow: "swifts just look like swifts--not like swallows."  And boom. Something that looked like a swift. Smaller, no real protruding tail feathers, and all dark. Tracked it for awhile in bins and then switched to camera and got some idable shots. Great last lifer for the trip

day long excursion to Sandy hook. targets were Whimbrel, American golden plover, and Philadelphia vireo.  not a huge day for passerines. overcast, except for around 2-4. hot then.  tide was still quite hi when I arrived at 12pm. spermcetti cove had black bellied plovers, SEPL, RUTU, but all distant.  explored north end mudflats next where tide was starting to recede. very few shorebirds but immense tern colony. sure to have been roseates mixed in with common but couldn't pick any out.  stayed until around 4pm, then walked the beach south down to the North Beach parking lot. eider was just offshore there, a long with a few piping plovers.  made another pass at sperm cove, this time with much of the mudflats exposed. more AMOY and BBPL now but no good American golden candidates.  went back to North end mudflats right around 530 and found two Whimbrel sitting right in the main leftover puddle on the flats. took most of my photos there and then watched them takeoff. they then flew back in, this time with 4 more, and did several aerial passes of the flats doing flight calls. pretty spectacular to watch. briefly touched down nearby for a few more photos and then left the area just before sunset.  successful and movie-esque day!

all morning search for Ms. wandering tattler  success in the final hour right before island packer.  More details:  Started at the jetty across from Island Packer lot. Wasn't having a ton of luck there, so drove to the other side of the creek mouth to scope from there, where I got absolutely nailed by a wave. Had to go to CVS to get lens cleaner to clean my scope, nocs, and glasses. Came back to the north side and continued scoping from safer locations away from waves. Still no luck with Tattler. Drove back to the south side of the creek mouth and checked the "surfers knoll" area, then back to the initial scoping spot across from Island Packers. There was a surfing competition going on, and one of the announcements was loud enough to scare up a flock of shorebirds previously tucked away in the rocky jetty. Out of this mostly white-wing striped crowd (willet, surfbird, turnstone, peep), there was one all dark-winged individual that I immediately clocked and stayed on with nocs. It flew across the beach in front of me and landed on the north shoreline, a little before the start of the jetty. I checked my sibley app and found that indeed the tattler had all dark wings, so sprinted up the beach with my scope and found the tattler blended in perfectly with the rocks. Was an awesome chase day with a skin-of-my-teeth rewarding ending as I had to go check in with the Island Packers boat 15 minutes later.

first big target bird of the trip.  parked at the airboat tour parking lot and began by checking the massive tree full of fish crow and grackles above the ramp. no cowbirds. walked north up the street and saw a few more grackle in between the houses. walked back south on the other side and got side tracked by egrets and herons.  then did a walk out to the west most road and saw my first female BH cowbird. seemed like a promising sign.  walked south from the airboat lot and found a tree with at least 6 roosting cowbirds in it. did a careful check of each but all had dark eyes and similar shape/beak shape. there were a lot of tangled nooks and crannies though, so I felt like it was possible I had missed some. chatted with a local and then walked back up to the parking area to check the big boat ramp tree. still no cowbirds.  walked BACK out to the west most road and found another small roost of cowbirds and grackles. most of the brown headed were all perched and not moving, but one was jumping from branch to branch and caught my eye. got enough of a peak at the face to see something was different with its eye. immediately grabbed camera and snapped some pics to reveal a red iris with a black pupil suspended in the middle.  glorious feeling. called Matt to tell him about it.  took a few more pics and then dipped cuz I thought everyone was probably sick of me walking through their neighborhood.  fun first lifer :)

***alright Rare but the circumstantial evidence piled up high enough for me to feel more confident about reporting this.  was walking in the trench on 161 at 6:12am and started looking up at two gull flyovers. then saw another bird flying WNW that looked like a DCCO but something felt off. Big broad wings but flapping slowly unlike a cormie with its typical panicked wing beats. More similar to a great blue.  checked it quick with bins and saw delicate brown streaking all down an otherwise pale neck. and the "neck" of what looked like a cormorant was actually the extremely long yellow beak of a tucked in heron head. Beak seemed way too long for a night heron. And the streaking was in high contrast with the paleness of the neck.  First gut instinct was omg it's a bittern. Camera wasn't even out of my bag so I fumbled for it and autofocus really shit the bed so I have photos of white sky.  Dm'ed a few folks about it and agreed it could only be Bittern or juv night heron.  Wasn't feeling confident enough to report it, but at 8:16 it was noted on Discord that Inwood Hill park had a bittern fly into it earlier in the morning. Asked for more details and learned it flew in at approximately 6:20-25am, which by my estimation lines up perfectly with my birds trajectory and timing (about 3 miles distance in 10/15 mins). This cinched it for me, so I'm updating my report.  Huge win for Macombs Dam Park (my trash park <3) and even more inspo to get up on the roof more frequently.

since i had missed my Vaux's Swift at bear divide earlier, i checked ebird for recent reports that were on the way from bear divide to ballona creek where i had to get that afternoon. Michael Klotz and Carli Wyllie had reported some at "Sepulveda Basin--East of Woodley Ave" on 4/16, so that became the next stop. Eyeballing the map, I thought the east basin close to the 405 would be the most likely spot, so I tried there first. TONS of swallows on the water, which I tried to photograph for quite awhile hoping to land a swift. But they were all foraging right on the water, whereas my gut was telling me a swift would prefer to be foraging high up in the air. After not turning up anything for about 30 minutes, I checked ebird once again and saw that a new report from Robert Thoren had just come in on 4/17 that there were two at the Lake Balboa hotspot on the other side of the park. I hightailed it over there, jumped out of the car and saw a MASSIVE flock of swallows circling above the parking lot. This seemed WAY more promising, as they were all up high. I ditched the camera for awhile and just stared up at different shapes, trying to remember what Matt told me last year when we were looking for a white throated swift when I asked him how he was able to tell apart a swift from a swallow: "swifts just look like swifts--not like swallows."  And boom. Something that looked like a swift. Smaller, no real protruding tail feathers, and all dark. Tracked it for awhile in bins and then switched to camera and got some idable shots. Great last lifer for the trip

day long excursion to Sandy hook. targets were Whimbrel, American golden plover, and Philadelphia vireo.  not a huge day for passerines. overcast, except for around 2-4. hot then.  tide was still quite hi when I arrived at 12pm. spermcetti cove had black bellied plovers, SEPL, RUTU, but all distant.  explored north end mudflats next where tide was starting to recede. very few shorebirds but immense tern colony. sure to have been roseates mixed in with common but couldn't pick any out.  stayed until around 4pm, then walked the beach south down to the North Beach parking lot. eider was just offshore there, a long with a few piping plovers.  made another pass at sperm cove, this time with much of the mudflats exposed. more AMOY and BBPL now but no good American golden candidates.  went back to North end mudflats right around 530 and found two Whimbrel sitting right in the main leftover puddle on the flats. took most of my photos there and then watched them takeoff. they then flew back in, this time with 4 more, and did several aerial passes of the flats doing flight calls. pretty spectacular to watch. briefly touched down nearby for a few more photos and then left the area just before sunset.  successful and movie-esque day!

Checklist Comments: absolutely stellar morning at Franz.  started at my usual spot mid park where it was a bit quiet and dark still. but heard what sounded like a great crested coming from the ball fields to the south. realized I never really check the tree line from INSIDE the ball fields, and have seen people running their dogs in there, so went to go check it out.  best decision of the day. immediately started hearing tons of warbler song, and the sun was hitting these southwest trees in full getting the bugs really active.  btgreen, mag, BTblue, yellow, and redstart were all quite readily found, a long with a vocal RBGR  biggest shocker came with a Wilson's warbler tucked deep in the lower branches. my first for the Bronx and a first of the year for me. huge win.  swallows came next with a glance at a tree swallow and good looks at a barn swallow.  hung around for an hour or so before exploring the rest of the park, which yielded some really close views of feeding Blackpolls in a reddish purple beech tree (thanks Jules)  gb heron flyover really cinched the morning.  wanted ovenbird and a thrush on the way out, so walked the Walton slopes and got my patch Swainsons :)))  most fire morning of the Franz season

CG: A sentimental birding moment for me. I missed the RI goose last winter, the one that foraged on the athletic fields of my high school. I’ve developed a strange attachment to it because there was something melancholic yet powerful about the idea of a vagrant from Eurasia standing among native Canadas on the very fields I walked across as a scared teenager when I first came to the US.    All year I kept hearing the question “did you go see the RI goose?” and even while birding in SF I coincidentally ran into Chelsea from NJ who took the goose photographs at the school: https://ebird.org/checklist/S211528327    Finally seeing this goose I’ve grown to identify with, here in my new home in NY with friends, feels deeply comforting.

since i had missed my Vaux's Swift at bear divide earlier, i checked ebird for recent reports that were on the way from bear divide to ballona creek where i had to get that afternoon. Michael Klotz and Carli Wyllie had reported some at "Sepulveda Basin--East of Woodley Ave" on 4/16, so that became the next stop. Eyeballing the map, I thought the east basin close to the 405 would be the most likely spot, so I tried there first. TONS of swallows on the water, which I tried to photograph for quite awhile hoping to land a swift. But they were all foraging right on the water, whereas my gut was telling me a swift would prefer to be foraging high up in the air. After not turning up anything for about 30 minutes, I checked ebird once again and saw that a new report from Robert Thoren had just come in on 4/17 that there were two at the Lake Balboa hotspot on the other side of the park. I hightailed it over there, jumped out of the car and saw a MASSIVE flock of swallows circling above the parking lot. This seemed WAY more promising, as they were all up high. I ditched the camera for awhile and just stared up at different shapes, trying to remember what Matt told me last year when we were looking for a white throated swift when I asked him how he was able to tell apart a swift from a swallow: "swifts just look like swifts--not like swallows."  And boom. Something that looked like a swift. Smaller, no real protruding tail feathers, and all dark. Tracked it for awhile in bins and then switched to camera and got some idable shots. Great last lifer for the trip

Arrived still in the dark to see one birder, Matt, already with his scope up. Did a few NYtimes games on my phone until it got slightly more reasonable of lighting conditions and joined him. Gorgeous view from up above the berm. Tons of dark shadow sleeping geese -- estimated at least a thousand by best guess.  Then the Where's Waldo game began as more light gave us more details on the birds. Over half were still sleeping. Scanned through the ones in the water many times as it would be most obvious there, but remained pretty sure it wasn't among them. Several trips to the car to refill coffee and add more layers of clothing, and the several more birders joined us.  At approximately 720ish, I caught a glimpse of white fringing on some wing feathers of a sleeping goose tucked in. I called it out and got everyone on it. Despite being almost entirely certain this HAD to be our tundra goose, I didn't want to post it to the Rhode Island groupme until it's head came untucked. And low and behold around 730, it did. I sent the alert out, the whole crew congratulated each other, and I believe Matt got back home in time for baseball.  Great to meet Danny and Ron. Super fun morning of sitting and watching the goose walk around, preen, swim, drink water, and take multiple naps.  Later in the morning I joined others closer down on the reservoir-edge berm. We watched it cozy up into a flock of sleeping canadas, and then I took my eyes off it for a moment, heard a commotion of a few geese flying, and completely lost it. it must've taken off right as I took my eyes off. Amazing bird and great way to celebrate the end of January recitals

all morning search for Ms. wandering tattler  success in the final hour right before island packer.  More details:  Started at the jetty across from Island Packer lot. Wasn't having a ton of luck there, so drove to the other side of the creek mouth to scope from there, where I got absolutely nailed by a wave. Had to go to CVS to get lens cleaner to clean my scope, nocs, and glasses. Came back to the north side and continued scoping from safer locations away from waves. Still no luck with Tattler. Drove back to the south side of the creek mouth and checked the "surfers knoll" area, then back to the initial scoping spot across from Island Packers. There was a surfing competition going on, and one of the announcements was loud enough to scare up a flock of shorebirds previously tucked away in the rocky jetty. Out of this mostly white-wing striped crowd (willet, surfbird, turnstone, peep), there was one all dark-winged individual that I immediately clocked and stayed on with nocs. It flew across the beach in front of me and landed on the north shoreline, a little before the start of the jetty. I checked my sibley app and found that indeed the tattler had all dark wings, so sprinted up the beach with my scope and found the tattler blended in perfectly with the rocks. Was an awesome chase day with a skin-of-my-teeth rewarding ending as I had to go check in with the Island Packers boat 15 minutes later.

day long excursion to Sandy hook. targets were Whimbrel, American golden plover, and Philadelphia vireo.  not a huge day for passerines. overcast, except for around 2-4. hot then.  tide was still quite hi when I arrived at 12pm. spermcetti cove had black bellied plovers, SEPL, RUTU, but all distant.  explored north end mudflats next where tide was starting to recede. very few shorebirds but immense tern colony. sure to have been roseates mixed in with common but couldn't pick any out.  stayed until around 4pm, then walked the beach south down to the North Beach parking lot. eider was just offshore there, a long with a few piping plovers.  made another pass at sperm cove, this time with much of the mudflats exposed. more AMOY and BBPL now but no good American golden candidates.  went back to North end mudflats right around 530 and found two Whimbrel sitting right in the main leftover puddle on the flats. took most of my photos there and then watched them takeoff. they then flew back in, this time with 4 more, and did several aerial passes of the flats doing flight calls. pretty spectacular to watch. briefly touched down nearby for a few more photos and then left the area just before sunset.  successful and movie-esque day!

Checklist Comments: 11:20-1ish stationary skywatch by her majesty  then a loop of the park  chatted with madeleine.  sick day can't stop me from getting two new park birds and one Bronx bird    so rip to birdcast: it officially turned off on november 15 and we wont be graced with her presence again until March 1.  seemed like an overall big migration night though with many bluebirds, pipits, and songbirds reported all over the city.  initial plan was to celebrate being done with work by waking up at sunrise and doing morning flight at franz, then drive to pelham to meet up with rich and alyssa. but a fever intervened and i spent the night shivering, falling asleep at 4 and finally waking up at 1030 to a lot of FOMO from reports all over the city of big bird movement.    felt marginally better though, so i bundled up, got a smoothie and a sandwich and plopped down in the grass on the watch hill for a stationary 1:30 min watch.  enormously successful with one flyover pipit (picked up by merlin and then me moments later). wish i had gotten eyes on him because he sounded VERY close. would've loved a pic. N to S flight.  alyssa then posted a bluebird at pelham and i got very salty because my cold thwarted my target bird bluebird plans. it didn't help that merlin told me bluebird was my bird of the day.  but literally as i was sending her a screenshot of my BotD and complaining that i'd never see one at franz, a tuwuwuwU call came out of the sky to the W of me. i glanced down at merlin and it agreed with me: tuwuwuWU for sure.  incredibly, i got eyes and photos on a flock of 8 of them as they flew north over the NW woods of the park.  pretty quiet after that excitement. i thought bluebird was a county bird for me, but it turns out i saw one last year at pelham (where i also met hailey for the first time). but still a franz bird is just as good.    this songbird flight gave way to a slow but steady movement of raptors. many TUVU, red tailed hawks, and a bunch of extremely high up buteos I couldn't make out. I was also watching the CT group me where there were more reports of Golden Eagles drifting towards NY.    black vulture, broad winged hawk, bald eagle, golden eagle, and red-shouldered hawk were all the targets as my brain switched to raptor mode.    and lo and behold, a red-shouldered came over with a sharpie and a RTHA. beautiful orange underneath with black and white fringing to the wings and a lovely banded tail. i was worried i wouldn't recognize one if it came by, so i took a ton of pics just to be sure, but my instincts were right.    overall an amazing outcome for a late start day. welcome new franz birds 128 and 129: eastern bluebird and red-shouldered hawk <3

Checklist Comments: Wanted to come back to Constance Darden trail after driving by the afternoon before. Was in search of red-cockaded woodpeckers. Walked along the southern property line and found a mixed flock of songbirds similar to the one I had the previous day: chickadees, nuthatches, creepers, titmice, and notably another single blue-headed vireo.  Things quieted down once I got back to the main trail and were completely silent while I staked out the observation deck for 30 minutes or so. No cockaded woodpeckers.  Also, the red-shouldered hawk was seen along the road on the way in.

Arrived at about 7:15am to start my thanksgiving red cockaded woodpecker search. Parked at the trailhead marked Lipford Path and walked clockwise around the loop. Very quiet at first. On the northwest corner of the loop in the more woodsy park there was a large mixed flock of passerines whose presence was made known by the trumpeting of a bunch of boisterous chickadees. They were outdone in intensity however by the golden crowned kinglets who were making an equally noisy racket. Tucked away amongst these little fellows however were two oddities: a brief appearance by a blue-headed vireo--only seen for a moment but enough to spot the blue head and white spectacles. Was immediately distracted by an almost neon yellow bird that shot past in the background of my binoculars. After a bit of searching through more kinglets, the yellow bird appeared again to show itself as a pine warbler. A larger bird than all the nearby kinglets, with a nice olive back and subtle facial marks contrasting its lemondrop belly.    After the passerine flock passed, it was back to searching for red-cockaded. The northern edge of the loop was quiet, other than a few gunshots from hunters and dogs howling. A pileated flew by in a brief shock of contrasting red, black, and white, which brought the woodpecker total up to 3 seen (downy, hairy, pileated) and two heard (red-bellied, flicker). But still no cockaded. As I turned south and began walking down the eastern edge of the loop I resigned myself to taking a coffee/food break and returning to search for the cockaded later. I sped up my walk a bit but paused when a group of white-throated sparrows and other passerines started making a racket again. That's when I started hearing the tapping of beaks on trees and saw a flurry of woodpecker-like movement in the pine treetops. A group of 5-6 red cockaded woodpeckers with bright white cheeks, an absence of black eye streaks, and dirty gray spotting down the flanks flew in and foraged in the north-east corner of the loop for almost an hour while I took very far away distant photos.    Hunger finally got to me and I decided to return to the car, but on the last leg of the loop I encountered a 2nd group of red-cockaded, with some even close enough to take decent photos of.    A huge success with two life birds for me--didn't even mention the brown-headed nuthatches. But they're dope too.

Returned to the same trail from 11/23/2023, but this time entered at the more eastern end of the loop and returned to the general location of the previous day's red-cockaded woodpeckers. Was there for about 30 minutes before hearing gentle tapping high up in the trees and a group of RCWO foraged their way into view. A lone downy woodpecker also tried to fake me out into thinking there was a RCWO 2 feet from me.  Another lemondrop yellow pine warbler showed up at one point. And a few bald eagles flew overhead (or possibly the same one circling). Lots of hunting gunshots--sort of eerie. The RCWO brought a nice calming feeling though.

day long excursion to Sandy hook. targets were Whimbrel, American golden plover, and Philadelphia vireo.  not a huge day for passerines. overcast, except for around 2-4. hot then.  tide was still quite hi when I arrived at 12pm. spermcetti cove had black bellied plovers, SEPL, RUTU, but all distant.  explored north end mudflats next where tide was starting to recede. very few shorebirds but immense tern colony. sure to have been roseates mixed in with common but couldn't pick any out.  stayed until around 4pm, then walked the beach south down to the North Beach parking lot. eider was just offshore there, a long with a few piping plovers.  made another pass at sperm cove, this time with much of the mudflats exposed. more AMOY and BBPL now but no good American golden candidates.  went back to North end mudflats right around 530 and found two Whimbrel sitting right in the main leftover puddle on the flats. took most of my photos there and then watched them takeoff. they then flew back in, this time with 4 more, and did several aerial passes of the flats doing flight calls. pretty spectacular to watch. briefly touched down nearby for a few more photos and then left the area just before sunset.  successful and movie-esque day!

Checklist Comments: 11:20-1ish stationary skywatch by her majesty  then a loop of the park  chatted with madeleine.  sick day can't stop me from getting two new park birds and one Bronx bird    so rip to birdcast: it officially turned off on november 15 and we wont be graced with her presence again until March 1.  seemed like an overall big migration night though with many bluebirds, pipits, and songbirds reported all over the city.  initial plan was to celebrate being done with work by waking up at sunrise and doing morning flight at franz, then drive to pelham to meet up with rich and alyssa. but a fever intervened and i spent the night shivering, falling asleep at 4 and finally waking up at 1030 to a lot of FOMO from reports all over the city of big bird movement.    felt marginally better though, so i bundled up, got a smoothie and a sandwich and plopped down in the grass on the watch hill for a stationary 1:30 min watch.  enormously successful with one flyover pipit (picked up by merlin and then me moments later). wish i had gotten eyes on him because he sounded VERY close. would've loved a pic. N to S flight.  alyssa then posted a bluebird at pelham and i got very salty because my cold thwarted my target bird bluebird plans. it didn't help that merlin told me bluebird was my bird of the day.  but literally as i was sending her a screenshot of my BotD and complaining that i'd never see one at franz, a tuwuwuwU call came out of the sky to the W of me. i glanced down at merlin and it agreed with me: tuwuwuWU for sure.  incredibly, i got eyes and photos on a flock of 8 of them as they flew north over the NW woods of the park.  pretty quiet after that excitement. i thought bluebird was a county bird for me, but it turns out i saw one last year at pelham (where i also met hailey for the first time). but still a franz bird is just as good.    this songbird flight gave way to a slow but steady movement of raptors. many TUVU, red tailed hawks, and a bunch of extremely high up buteos I couldn't make out. I was also watching the CT group me where there were more reports of Golden Eagles drifting towards NY.    black vulture, broad winged hawk, bald eagle, golden eagle, and red-shouldered hawk were all the targets as my brain switched to raptor mode.    and lo and behold, a red-shouldered came over with a sharpie and a RTHA. beautiful orange underneath with black and white fringing to the wings and a lovely banded tail. i was worried i wouldn't recognize one if it came by, so i took a ton of pics just to be sure, but my instincts were right.    overall an amazing outcome for a late start day. welcome new franz birds 128 and 129: eastern bluebird and red-shouldered hawk <3

Observation Details: hunting in the park
Checklist Comments: 11:20-1ish stationary skywatch by her majesty  then a loop of the park  chatted with madeleine.  sick day can't stop me from getting two new park birds and one Bronx bird    so rip to birdcast: it officially turned off on november 15 and we wont be graced with her presence again until March 1.  seemed like an overall big migration night though with many bluebirds, pipits, and songbirds reported all over the city.  initial plan was to celebrate being done with work by waking up at sunrise and doing morning flight at franz, then drive to pelham to meet up with rich and alyssa. but a fever intervened and i spent the night shivering, falling asleep at 4 and finally waking up at 1030 to a lot of FOMO from reports all over the city of big bird movement.    felt marginally better though, so i bundled up, got a smoothie and a sandwich and plopped down in the grass on the watch hill for a stationary 1:30 min watch.  enormously successful with one flyover pipit (picked up by merlin and then me moments later). wish i had gotten eyes on him because he sounded VERY close. would've loved a pic. N to S flight.  alyssa then posted a bluebird at pelham and i got very salty because my cold thwarted my target bird bluebird plans. it didn't help that merlin told me bluebird was my bird of the day.  but literally as i was sending her a screenshot of my BotD and complaining that i'd never see one at franz, a tuwuwuwU call came out of the sky to the W of me. i glanced down at merlin and it agreed with me: tuwuwuWU for sure.  incredibly, i got eyes and photos on a flock of 8 of them as they flew north over the NW woods of the park.  pretty quiet after that excitement. i thought bluebird was a county bird for me, but it turns out i saw one last year at pelham (where i also met hailey for the first time). but still a franz bird is just as good.    this songbird flight gave way to a slow but steady movement of raptors. many TUVU, red tailed hawks, and a bunch of extremely high up buteos I couldn't make out. I was also watching the CT group me where there were more reports of Golden Eagles drifting towards NY.    black vulture, broad winged hawk, bald eagle, golden eagle, and red-shouldered hawk were all the targets as my brain switched to raptor mode.    and lo and behold, a red-shouldered came over with a sharpie and a RTHA. beautiful orange underneath with black and white fringing to the wings and a lovely banded tail. i was worried i wouldn't recognize one if it came by, so i took a ton of pics just to be sure, but my instincts were right.    overall an amazing outcome for a late start day. welcome new franz birds 128 and 129: eastern bluebird and red-shouldered hawk <3

Checklist Comments: incredibly risky chase for a incredibly rare bird.  checked the Wilbur avenue fields where it was seen in the late afternoon of January 13 first. Was still dark out but could tell there were no roosting birds--which makes sense--i would prefer water as well.  Next stop was a pin on Salem Street parallel to the Batten Kill river. Through the houses I could see there was a decent number 40+ geese on the ice. Sent out a quick message on discord that geese were present. But viewing conditions were hard as the geese were further west of the pin and it was on a residential street. After a few attempts at scoping the geese in between houses (and a dirty look from a woman in her kitchen), I decided to hustle over to the opposite side of the river to try a different vantage point. Drove a little too fast through sleepy Greenwich.  Saw the name Rock Street and headed down that way to the PERFECT vantage point. And lo and behold there were about 150 more geese bathing on the north side of the river that was previously unviewable from the Salem pin. I excitedly started scanning and didn't see any non-canada at first. No yellow/orange bills poked out through the sea of black/white/and gray. And then boom -- noticed an all gray head that didn't match the  CANG. stayed on it while it faced away from me, then watched it turn and cinched the ID with the black/orange bill. Immediately skipped a heartbeat, digiscoped a shot and sent the pic and co-ords to discord at 7:18am.  I stayed for roughly two more hours and watched it swim, feed, drink water, get spooked by eagles, climb up on the ice, do a few wing flaps, and take about a 35 minute nap.  Was joined soon after finding it by Barbara Mansell, Debbie van Zyl, and Zach Shaoul. Lovely time chatting with them and bonding over this amazing bird, and later with Bob Proniewych from Nassau county.  Back in the city by 1pm and ready for a nap.

all day on the mountain checklist. details of notable birds and where they were seen in list. skill checked by pinyon jays.  chuck and Jenn motorcycle broz nice to meet ya    More notes:  I was cranky from my earlier pinyon jay search on the west side of highway 395, so why not spend the rest of the day looking over the entirety of White Mountain for pinyon jays?  This checklist is kind of all encompassing of White Mountain. Started at the flats off the highway, continued up to the grandview campground where I finally saw a mountain bluebird undeniably, then up to the bristlecone pine forest where I had my socks blown off by those trees. Unexpectedly ran into more Williamsons Sapsuckers up there which was a treat. But no Pinyon Jays, despite even playing their call a bit from my car speakers. The other target was a Clark's Nutcracker, which was beginning to feel like a no go, but finally got it on the dirt road past the bristle forest on my way back down.

lazy checklist for the whole mountain trek. started at cedar flats and drove up to bristlecone lot and back down. searching for pinyon jay the whole time but no luck.  gray flycatcher was a lifer at Grandview though so worth it 😎    Weird start to the day. I thought it would be cool to hear a Pygmy Owl at Glacier Lodge, so I drove up there around 4 and listened. Nothing. Was going to start using playback and then was like "what am i doing" so    drove back down and got coffee at Brewed Awakenings (thanks for being open at 5). Unsatisfied with my 5 hours of pinyon jay searching the previous day, I decided to give it another morning.   The itinerary at this point was to drive back to Lancaster today, stopping along the way, and then wake up on Thursday to find a LeConte's thrasher before driving into LA to return my car that afternoon. So what basically I had a full day to kill, minus the 3.5 hour drive to Lancaster.  Basically repeated the previous day's path--started at Cedar Flats photographing some Junipers, went up to Grandview Campground (where I had my lifer Gray Flycatcher), took an extended stop at the Vista View, then up to Bristlecone for a brief walk around. I stopped every quarter mile or so on the road to listen for Pinyon Jays on the way up and the way down. Nothing doing. Cool flyby Clarks at Vista View. But overall a tough strike out on Jays.

since i had missed my Vaux's Swift at bear divide earlier, i checked ebird for recent reports that were on the way from bear divide to ballona creek where i had to get that afternoon. Michael Klotz and Carli Wyllie had reported some at "Sepulveda Basin--East of Woodley Ave" on 4/16, so that became the next stop. Eyeballing the map, I thought the east basin close to the 405 would be the most likely spot, so I tried there first. TONS of swallows on the water, which I tried to photograph for quite awhile hoping to land a swift. But they were all foraging right on the water, whereas my gut was telling me a swift would prefer to be foraging high up in the air. After not turning up anything for about 30 minutes, I checked ebird once again and saw that a new report from Robert Thoren had just come in on 4/17 that there were two at the Lake Balboa hotspot on the other side of the park. I hightailed it over there, jumped out of the car and saw a MASSIVE flock of swallows circling above the parking lot. This seemed WAY more promising, as they were all up high. I ditched the camera for awhile and just stared up at different shapes, trying to remember what Matt told me last year when we were looking for a white throated swift when I asked him how he was able to tell apart a swift from a swallow: "swifts just look like swifts--not like swallows."  And boom. Something that looked like a swift. Smaller, no real protruding tail feathers, and all dark. Tracked it for awhile in bins and then switched to camera and got some idable shots. Great last lifer for the trip

Location: Owens River Rd.--1 mile east of  Hwy 395
Checklist Comments: so after a grouse morning, the plan was to hit up some different spots that people had recently seen red-naped and williamson's sapsuckers.  The first stop was going to be Hartley Springs Campground where Alvin and Ellen had a pair on 04/04, but when I got there I saw it was a snow covered road and I wasn't about to brave it in my rental with no snow tires. The next option was Twin Lakes Campground, where Colin Danch had one on 04/14. It was going to be a long drive and I was a little bummed out that I have driven 35 minutes north already just to get to a closed road. But as I was driving south again, I noticed I was near the hotspot "Owens River Rd.--1 mile east of Hwy 395" which I recognized from Steve Glover and Darlene McNeil's trip report from a few years ago. I decided since it was on my way, I'd poke in quickly since they had Williamson's here years ago. Plus Grub Fay had reported one in January of this year. Popped in and within 15 minutes had a Williamsons pair drumming. Amazingly fortunate and felt really smiled upon by the universe. All that spreadsheet work paid off!  Lifer cassin's finch female was also here, along with tons of fun red crossbills, brown creepers, chickadees, MORE white-headed woodpeckers, and merlin even picked up an Evening Grosbeak, but I didn't see it so not listing it.

quick drive around looking for pinyon jays/mountain bluebirds  More:  Pinyon Jay search continued with a slow drive down Old Sherwin Grade Road, and eventually up to Swall Meadows. I thought this place was going to be more of a big park, but it's basically just a town. And with a lot of No Trespassing signs on meadow roads. So this was a little unfortunate. Did a long drive of most of the town roads listening for a Pinyon flock or perhaps a mountain bluebird, but got discouraged and gave up.  The next stop was, which I didn't make a checklist for, was in the town of Paradise at the Lower Rock Creek Trailhead. This was very unclearly marked, and I tried walking a little bit down the "trail" just to wind up in someone's driveway. I'm sure I missed something indicating where the trail was, but this felt very discouraging and made me wish things were a little better marked for visiting birders.  Also of note from earlier: if you try to Google Maps your way to the "Lower Rock Creek" hotspot, it'll tell you to take a closed road off of 395 around here:  37.519876, -118.611409  Pretty unhelpful ebird hotspot locations in general. I was getting cranky.

Checklist Comments: 11:20-1ish stationary skywatch by her majesty  then a loop of the park  chatted with madeleine.  sick day can't stop me from getting two new park birds and one Bronx bird    so rip to birdcast: it officially turned off on november 15 and we wont be graced with her presence again until March 1.  seemed like an overall big migration night though with many bluebirds, pipits, and songbirds reported all over the city.  initial plan was to celebrate being done with work by waking up at sunrise and doing morning flight at franz, then drive to pelham to meet up with rich and alyssa. but a fever intervened and i spent the night shivering, falling asleep at 4 and finally waking up at 1030 to a lot of FOMO from reports all over the city of big bird movement.    felt marginally better though, so i bundled up, got a smoothie and a sandwich and plopped down in the grass on the watch hill for a stationary 1:30 min watch.  enormously successful with one flyover pipit (picked up by merlin and then me moments later). wish i had gotten eyes on him because he sounded VERY close. would've loved a pic. N to S flight.  alyssa then posted a bluebird at pelham and i got very salty because my cold thwarted my target bird bluebird plans. it didn't help that merlin told me bluebird was my bird of the day.  but literally as i was sending her a screenshot of my BotD and complaining that i'd never see one at franz, a tuwuwuwU call came out of the sky to the W of me. i glanced down at merlin and it agreed with me: tuwuwuWU for sure.  incredibly, i got eyes and photos on a flock of 8 of them as they flew north over the NW woods of the park.  pretty quiet after that excitement. i thought bluebird was a county bird for me, but it turns out i saw one last year at pelham (where i also met hailey for the first time). but still a franz bird is just as good.    this songbird flight gave way to a slow but steady movement of raptors. many TUVU, red tailed hawks, and a bunch of extremely high up buteos I couldn't make out. I was also watching the CT group me where there were more reports of Golden Eagles drifting towards NY.    black vulture, broad winged hawk, bald eagle, golden eagle, and red-shouldered hawk were all the targets as my brain switched to raptor mode.    and lo and behold, a red-shouldered came over with a sharpie and a RTHA. beautiful orange underneath with black and white fringing to the wings and a lovely banded tail. i was worried i wouldn't recognize one if it came by, so i took a ton of pics just to be sure, but my instincts were right.    overall an amazing outcome for a late start day. welcome new franz birds 128 and 129: eastern bluebird and red-shouldered hawk <3

Observation Details: insane.  first eBird record in the west bronx.  high up, getting mobbed by crows, and power-coasting east.  white bird with smushed in head, short fanned tail, and brown streaking on breast. photos and more details later    ***okay SO  this looks to be the 12th Bronx record of SEowl. but most notable, it's the only inland record (the others come entirely from Pelham and ferry point, in more suitable habitat)    absolutely nutso to see one in such a dense urban environment. I have not seen so many ravens together here before either, which makes me think perhaps it was following the Harlem River/Hudson down when the Ravens caught onto its tail and started mobbing it and steered it off course? Because I doubt an SEowl is willingly migrating over the grand concourse.  ***got a tip that these were in fact crows, not ravens. I assumed short eared owls were large, but it turns out they're only 14/15 inches in length, just smaller than a crow. ravens would be 24/25    anyways was about 8:00am exactly when I was coming up to the rocky hill looking at sparrows to do another north end loop. Luci saw me from far away and dashed over to say hi and I wound up chatting with Tania for awhile about some work drama.    Cut her off in the middle of a sentence when I looked up and saw an all white bird in the midst of about 6 crows. "is that a fucking owl" I said out loud and Tania asked if I meant the white one. I got camera shots of it for maybe 30 seconds while it looped around and then headed off east (hopefully to better east Bronx habitat or Suffolk).    Franz Sigel park's official second owl (counting the 1953 saw whet owl by PA Buckley). And notably we got a short eared owl on eBird before central park >:)))    bird #127 for the park and #195 for me for the BX

since i had missed my Vaux's Swift at bear divide earlier, i checked ebird for recent reports that were on the way from bear divide to ballona creek where i had to get that afternoon. Michael Klotz and Carli Wyllie had reported some at "Sepulveda Basin--East of Woodley Ave" on 4/16, so that became the next stop. Eyeballing the map, I thought the east basin close to the 405 would be the most likely spot, so I tried there first. TONS of swallows on the water, which I tried to photograph for quite awhile hoping to land a swift. But they were all foraging right on the water, whereas my gut was telling me a swift would prefer to be foraging high up in the air. After not turning up anything for about 30 minutes, I checked ebird once again and saw that a new report from Robert Thoren had just come in on 4/17 that there were two at the Lake Balboa hotspot on the other side of the park. I hightailed it over there, jumped out of the car and saw a MASSIVE flock of swallows circling above the parking lot. This seemed WAY more promising, as they were all up high. I ditched the camera for awhile and just stared up at different shapes, trying to remember what Matt told me last year when we were looking for a white throated swift when I asked him how he was able to tell apart a swift from a swallow: "swifts just look like swifts--not like swallows."  And boom. Something that looked like a swift. Smaller, no real protruding tail feathers, and all dark. Tracked it for awhile in bins and then switched to camera and got some idable shots. Great last lifer for the trip

day long excursion to Sandy hook. targets were Whimbrel, American golden plover, and Philadelphia vireo.  not a huge day for passerines. overcast, except for around 2-4. hot then.  tide was still quite hi when I arrived at 12pm. spermcetti cove had black bellied plovers, SEPL, RUTU, but all distant.  explored north end mudflats next where tide was starting to recede. very few shorebirds but immense tern colony. sure to have been roseates mixed in with common but couldn't pick any out.  stayed until around 4pm, then walked the beach south down to the North Beach parking lot. eider was just offshore there, a long with a few piping plovers.  made another pass at sperm cove, this time with much of the mudflats exposed. more AMOY and BBPL now but no good American golden candidates.  went back to North end mudflats right around 530 and found two Whimbrel sitting right in the main leftover puddle on the flats. took most of my photos there and then watched them takeoff. they then flew back in, this time with 4 more, and did several aerial passes of the flats doing flight calls. pretty spectacular to watch. briefly touched down nearby for a few more photos and then left the area just before sunset.  successful and movie-esque day!

This checklist is kind of all encompassing of White Mountain. Started at the flats off the highway, continued up to the grandview campground where I finally saw a mountain bluebird undeniably, then up to the bristlecone pine forest where I had my socks blown off by those trees. Unexpectedly ran into more Williamsons Sapsuckers up there which was a treat. But no Pinyon Jays, despite even playing their call a bit from my car speakers. The other target was a Clark's Nutcracker, which was beginning to feel like a no go, but finally got it on the dirt road past the bristle forest on my way back down.

I thought it would be cool to hear a Pygmy Owl at Glacier Lodge, so I drove up there around 4 and listened. Nothing. Was going to start using playback and then was like "what am i doing" so    drove back down and got coffee at Brewed Awakenings (thanks for being open at 5). Unsatisfied with my 5 hours of pinyon jay searching the previous day, I decided to give it another morning.   The itinerary at this point was to drive back to Lancaster today, stopping along the way, and then wake up on Thursday to find a LeConte's thrasher before driving into LA to return my car that afternoon. So what basically I had a full day to kill, minus the 3.5 hour drive to Lancaster.  Basically repeated the previous day's path--started at Cedar Flats photographing some Junipers, went up to Grandview Campground (where I had my lifer Gray Flycatcher), took an extended stop at the Vista View, then up to Bristlecone for a brief walk around.
