lifer! deets and photos to come  pulled up to turkey flats and cholame intersection and only saw/heard acorn woodpeckers and titmice. did a thorough check of the trees all around the intersection and didn't see anything else.  then walked slightly down the road to:  35°52'38.4"N 120°25'03.5"W  where an earlier report had tagged them and found two in the trees. they seemed to be in a little bit of a scuff with the acorn woodpeckers, trading positions and barking at each other a bit. the lewis's mostly stayed in the shadows of one large leafy tree, but occasionally would come out and perch on some large dead trees or the telephone pole. i took photos of the spot they were if anyone is having trouble finding them and wants to email me.  huge thanks to Rich Freese and Karen Kreiger for keeping continuing reports of these birds going in 2025 and a HUGE thanks to Will Knowlton	for the confirmed sighting on 04/10. I almost wasn't going to make the trek up to Monterey county since it seemed like they might not stay, but I checked the species map just in the nick of time on the night of April 12 and saw Will's report. Just shows how important adding your sightings to eBird is--can really make someone's day. Final US Woodpecker, not counting sapsuckers :)  stay the course guys--you're doing super!

Observation Details: awesome long-awaited pick up for the year. thanks to julian elman for posting its coords on discord. arrived and found it shortly after flying around with a red-bellied woodpecker, making a circuit of three or four trees on near leonard bernstein's grave. First caught it in flight by seeing its bold white wing panels which i'd never gotten a good look at before. Really glorious and noticeable, even at a quick glance. Went and searched for a connecticut warbler and then returned an hour later to find it in a nearby tree, still associating with a red-bellied. i staked it out for about an hour trying to get some good shots of it when much to my surprise it split into two! i believe i was able to get shots of both: you can see in these photos that the bird perched with its back to the camera and its head turned left has quite a dark back, whereas the other individual has a long more white fringing on the feathers, giving it a more mottled look. there also seems to be more black barring feathers in the white wing panels on one individual. both seemed to be foraging in nearby trees with each other, and when one would take flight the other would follow. observed flycatching at one point which was a treat--never seen that behavior before.  year bird #467!

11:20-1ish stationary skywatch by her majesty  then a loop of the park  chatted with madeleine.  sick day can't stop me from getting two new park birds and one Bronx bird    so rip to birdcast: it officially turned off on november 15 and we wont be graced with her presence again until March 1.  seemed like an overall big migration night though with many bluebirds, pipits, and songbirds reported all over the city.  initial plan was to celebrate being done with work by waking up at sunrise and doing morning flight at franz, then drive to pelham to meet up with rich and alyssa. but a fever intervened and i spent the night shivering, falling asleep at 4 and finally waking up at 1030 to a lot of FOMO from reports all over the city of big bird movement.    felt marginally better though, so i bundled up, got a smoothie and a sandwich and plopped down in the grass on the watch hill for a stationary 1:30 min watch.  enormously successful with one flyover pipit (picked up by merlin and then me moments later). wish i had gotten eyes on him because he sounded VERY close. would've loved a pic. N to S flight.  alyssa then posted a bluebird at pelham and i got very salty because my cold thwarted my target bird bluebird plans. it didn't help that merlin told me bluebird was my bird of the day.  but literally as i was sending her a screenshot of my BotD and complaining that i'd never see one at franz, a tuwuwuwU call came out of the sky to the W of me. i glanced down at merlin and it agreed with me: tuwuwuWU for sure.  incredibly, i got eyes and photos on a flock of 8 of them as they flew north over the NW woods of the park.  pretty quiet after that excitement. i thought bluebird was a county bird for me, but it turns out i saw one last year at pelham (where i also met hailey for the first time). but still a franz bird is just as good.    this songbird flight gave way to a slow but steady movement of raptors. many TUVU, red tailed hawks, and a bunch of extremely high up buteos I couldn't make out. I was also watching the CT group me where there were more reports of Golden Eagles drifting towards NY.    black vulture, broad winged hawk, bald eagle, golden eagle, and red-shouldered hawk were all the targets as my brain switched to raptor mode.    and lo and behold, a red-shouldered came over with a sharpie and a RTHA. beautiful orange underneath with black and white fringing to the wings and a lovely banded tail. i was worried i wouldn't recognize one if it came by, so i took a ton of pics just to be sure, but my instincts were right.    overall an amazing outcome for a late start day. welcome new franz birds 128 and 129: eastern bluebird and red-shouldered hawk <3

CG: A sentimental birding moment for me. I missed the RI goose last winter, the one that foraged on the athletic fields of my high school. I’ve developed a strange attachment to it because there was something melancholic yet powerful about the idea of a vagrant from Eurasia standing among native Canadas on the very fields I walked across as a scared teenager when I first came to the US.    All year I kept hearing the question “did you go see the RI goose?” and even while birding in SF I coincidentally ran into Chelsea from NJ who took the goose photographs at the school: https://ebird.org/checklist/S211528327    Finally seeing this goose I’ve grown to identify with, here in my new home in NY with friends, feels deeply comforting.

Checklist Comments: incredibly risky chase for a incredibly rare bird.  checked the Wilbur avenue fields where it was seen in the late afternoon of January 13 first. Was still dark out but could tell there were no roosting birds--which makes sense--i would prefer water as well.  Next stop was a pin on Salem Street parallel to the Batten Kill river. Through the houses I could see there was a decent number 40+ geese on the ice. Sent out a quick message on discord that geese were present. But viewing conditions were hard as the geese were further west of the pin and it was on a residential street. After a few attempts at scoping the geese in between houses (and a dirty look from a woman in her kitchen), I decided to hustle over to the opposite side of the river to try a different vantage point. Drove a little too fast through sleepy Greenwich.  Saw the name Rock Street and headed down that way to the PERFECT vantage point. And lo and behold there were about 150 more geese bathing on the north side of the river that was previously unviewable from the Salem pin. I excitedly started scanning and didn't see any non-canada at first. No yellow/orange bills poked out through the sea of black/white/and gray. And then boom -- noticed an all gray head that didn't match the  CANG. stayed on it while it faced away from me, then watched it turn and cinched the ID with the black/orange bill. Immediately skipped a heartbeat, digiscoped a shot and sent the pic and co-ords to discord at 7:18am.  I stayed for roughly two more hours and watched it swim, feed, drink water, get spooked by eagles, climb up on the ice, do a few wing flaps, and take about a 35 minute nap.  Was joined soon after finding it by Barbara Mansell, Debbie van Zyl, and Zach Shaoul. Lovely time chatting with them and bonding over this amazing bird, and later with Bob Proniewych from Nassau county.  Back in the city by 1pm and ready for a nap.

Arrived at about 7:15am to start my thanksgiving red cockaded woodpecker search. Parked at the trailhead marked Lipford Path and walked clockwise around the loop. Very quiet at first. On the northwest corner of the loop in the more woodsy park there was a large mixed flock of passerines whose presence was made known by the trumpeting of a bunch of boisterous chickadees. They were outdone in intensity however by the golden crowned kinglets who were making an equally noisy racket. Tucked away amongst these little fellows however were two oddities: a brief appearance by a blue-headed vireo--only seen for a moment but enough to spot the blue head and white spectacles. Was immediately distracted by an almost neon yellow bird that shot past in the background of my binoculars. After a bit of searching through more kinglets, the yellow bird appeared again to show itself as a pine warbler. A larger bird than all the nearby kinglets, with a nice olive back and subtle facial marks contrasting its lemondrop belly.    After the passerine flock passed, it was back to searching for red-cockaded. The northern edge of the loop was quiet, other than a few gunshots from hunters and dogs howling. A pileated flew by in a brief shock of contrasting red, black, and white, which brought the woodpecker total up to 3 seen (downy, hairy, pileated) and two heard (red-bellied, flicker). But still no cockaded. As I turned south and began walking down the eastern edge of the loop I resigned myself to taking a coffee/food break and returning to search for the cockaded later. I sped up my walk a bit but paused when a group of white-throated sparrows and other passerines started making a racket again. That's when I started hearing the tapping of beaks on trees and saw a flurry of woodpecker-like movement in the pine treetops. A group of 5-6 red cockaded woodpeckers with bright white cheeks, an absence of black eye streaks, and dirty gray spotting down the flanks flew in and foraged in the north-east corner of the loop for almost an hour while I took very far away distant photos.    Hunger finally got to me and I decided to return to the car, but on the last leg of the loop I encountered a 2nd group of red-cockaded, with some even close enough to take decent photos of.    A huge success with two life birds for me--didn't even mention the brown-headed nuthatches. But they're dope too.

Returned to the same trail from 11/23/2023, but this time entered at the more eastern end of the loop and returned to the general location of the previous day's red-cockaded woodpeckers. Was there for about 30 minutes before hearing gentle tapping high up in the trees and a group of RCWO foraged their way into view. A lone downy woodpecker also tried to fake me out into thinking there was a RCWO 2 feet from me.  Another lemondrop yellow pine warbler showed up at one point. And a few bald eagles flew overhead (or possibly the same one circling). Lots of hunting gunshots--sort of eerie. The RCWO brought a nice calming feeling though.

11:20-1ish stationary skywatch by her majesty  then a loop of the park  chatted with madeleine.  sick day can't stop me from getting two new park birds and one Bronx bird    so rip to birdcast: it officially turned off on november 15 and we wont be graced with her presence again until March 1.  seemed like an overall big migration night though with many bluebirds, pipits, and songbirds reported all over the city.  initial plan was to celebrate being done with work by waking up at sunrise and doing morning flight at franz, then drive to pelham to meet up with rich and alyssa. but a fever intervened and i spent the night shivering, falling asleep at 4 and finally waking up at 1030 to a lot of FOMO from reports all over the city of big bird movement.    felt marginally better though, so i bundled up, got a smoothie and a sandwich and plopped down in the grass on the watch hill for a stationary 1:30 min watch.  enormously successful with one flyover pipit (picked up by merlin and then me moments later). wish i had gotten eyes on him because he sounded VERY close. would've loved a pic. N to S flight.  alyssa then posted a bluebird at pelham and i got very salty because my cold thwarted my target bird bluebird plans. it didn't help that merlin told me bluebird was my bird of the day.  but literally as i was sending her a screenshot of my BotD and complaining that i'd never see one at franz, a tuwuwuwU call came out of the sky to the W of me. i glanced down at merlin and it agreed with me: tuwuwuWU for sure.  incredibly, i got eyes and photos on a flock of 8 of them as they flew north over the NW woods of the park.  pretty quiet after that excitement. i thought bluebird was a county bird for me, but it turns out i saw one last year at pelham (where i also met hailey for the first time). but still a franz bird is just as good.    this songbird flight gave way to a slow but steady movement of raptors. many TUVU, red tailed hawks, and a bunch of extremely high up buteos I couldn't make out. I was also watching the CT group me where there were more reports of Golden Eagles drifting towards NY.    black vulture, broad winged hawk, bald eagle, golden eagle, and red-shouldered hawk were all the targets as my brain switched to raptor mode.    and lo and behold, a red-shouldered came over with a sharpie and a RTHA. beautiful orange underneath with black and white fringing to the wings and a lovely banded tail. i was worried i wouldn't recognize one if it came by, so i took a ton of pics just to be sure, but my instincts were right.    overall an amazing outcome for a late start day. welcome new franz birds 128 and 129: eastern bluebird and red-shouldered hawk <3

Location: Grand Marais RV Park and Campground
Checklist Comments: lots of Bohemian Waxwing details later  okay so this was by far my longest stakeout. tried the previous afternoon and not a single waxwing appeared from 12:30-sunset.  day two i showed up in the morning and it was dead silent for about an hour. Was parked by the bathrooms/boats/baseball field area by the coke machine.  At 8:09am a small flock of waxwings flew over but did not stop. They flew in from the south and headed north towards the west side of Grand Marais. Then about 15 minutes later with the windows down I heard a single bird making a trilling call in the pines near the baseball field. I drove around the RV park looking for the single bird but couldn't find him, did a lap of the west side neighborhood to check the fruiting trees, and then returned to my stakeout.  At 8:49 a slightly larger flock finally flew in, doing large circles of the ball field area. I jumped out of the car and snapped flight photos, assuming they wouldn't stop again. Looking through these photos I can confirm some bohemians were present. But this time they alighted on a tall pine quite distant, adjacent to the baseball field (I snapped a photo of the tree in question later with a blue jay on it to give some reference--check the bluejay pic).  This was a small flock still--maybe 40 birds. But there were at least 4 bohemians mixed in. Got a few more photos and then the bohemians departed, leaving the cedar flock only. They never came down to the fruiting berries to eat, even though it was snowing and cold. I hung around until about 10:30 but only a small flock of CEWA ever showed up again. Not nearly the large flock numbers of 200+ people have been reporting.  Definitely a huge test of patience but super rewarding to get this dope lifer.

Checklist Comments: Arrived at about 7:15am to start my thanksgiving red cockaded woodpecker search. Parked at the trailhead marked Lipford Path and walked clockwise around the loop. Very quiet at first. On the northwest corner of the loop in the more woodsy park there was a large mixed flock of passerines whose presence was made known by the trumpeting of a bunch of boisterous chickadees. They were outdone in intensity however by the golden crowned kinglets who were making an equally noisy racket. Tucked away amongst these little fellows however were two oddities: a brief appearance by a blue-headed vireo--only seen for a moment but enough to spot the blue head and white spectacles. Was immediately distracted by an almost neon yellow bird that shot past in the background of my binoculars. After a bit of searching through more kinglets, the yellow bird appeared again to show itself as a pine warbler. A larger bird than all the nearby kinglets, with a nice olive back and subtle facial marks contrasting its lemondrop belly.    After the passerine flock passed, it was back to searching for red-cockaded. The northern edge of the loop was quiet, other than a few gunshots from hunters and dogs howling. A pileated flew by in a brief shock of contrasting red, black, and white, which brought the woodpecker total up to 3 seen (downy, hairy, pileated) and two heard (red-bellied, flicker). But still no cockaded. As I turned south and began walking down the eastern edge of the loop I resigned myself to taking a coffee/food break and returning to search for the cockaded later. I sped up my walk a bit but paused when a group of white-throated sparrows and other passerines started making a racket again. That's when I started hearing the tapping of beaks on trees and saw a flurry of woodpecker-like movement in the pine treetops. A group of 5-6 red cockaded woodpeckers with bright white cheeks, an absence of black eye streaks, and dirty gray spotting down the flanks flew in and foraged in the north-east corner of the loop for almost an hour while I took very far away distant photos.    Hunger finally got to me and I decided to return to the car, but on the last leg of the loop I encountered a 2nd group of red-cockaded, with some even close enough to take decent photos of.    A huge success with two life birds for me--didn't even mention the brown-headed nuthatches. But they're dope too.

Returned to the same trail from 11/23/2023, but this time entered at the more eastern end of the loop and returned to the general location of the previous day's red-cockaded woodpeckers. Was there for about 30 minutes before hearing gentle tapping high up in the trees and a group of RCWO foraged their way into view. A lone downy woodpecker also tried to fake me out into thinking there was a RCWO 2 feet from me.  Another lemondrop yellow pine warbler showed up at one point. And a few bald eagles flew overhead (or possibly the same one circling). Lots of hunting gunshots--sort of eerie. The RCWO brought a nice calming feeling though.

Location: Owens River Rd.--1 mile east of  Hwy 395
Observation Details: nice bonus find after the sapsuckers
Checklist Comments: so after a grouse morning, the plan was to hit up some different spots that people had recently seen red-naped and williamson's sapsuckers.  The first stop was going to be Hartley Springs Campground where Alvin and Ellen had a pair on 04/04, but when I got there I saw it was a snow covered road and I wasn't about to brave it in my rental with no snow tires. The next option was Twin Lakes Campground, where Colin Danch had one on 04/14. It was going to be a long drive and I was a little bummed out that I have driven 35 minutes north already just to get to a closed road. But as I was driving south again, I noticed I was near the hotspot "Owens River Rd.--1 mile east of Hwy 395" which I recognized from Steve Glover and Darlene McNeil's trip report from a few years ago. I decided since it was on my way, I'd poke in quickly since they had Williamson's here years ago. Plus Grub Fay had reported one in January of this year. Popped in and within 15 minutes had a Williamsons pair drumming. Amazingly fortunate and felt really smiled upon by the universe. All that spreadsheet work paid off!  Lifer cassin's finch female was also here, along with tons of fun red crossbills, brown creepers, chickadees, MORE white-headed woodpeckers, and merlin even picked up an Evening Grosbeak, but I didn't see it so not listing it.

Location: Carrie Nation Mine Trail, Green Valley, Arizona, US (31.71, -110.875)
Grand Marais RV Park and Campground
Observation Details: heard
Checklist Comments: lots of Bohemian Waxwing details later  okay so this was by far my longest stakeout. tried the previous afternoon and not a single waxwing appeared from 12:30-sunset.  day two i showed up in the morning and it was dead silent for about an hour. Was parked by the bathrooms/boats/baseball field area by the coke machine.  At 8:09am a small flock of waxwings flew over but did not stop. They flew in from the south and headed north towards the west side of Grand Marais. Then about 15 minutes later with the windows down I heard a single bird making a trilling call in the pines near the baseball field. I drove around the RV park looking for the single bird but couldn't find him, did a lap of the west side neighborhood to check the fruiting trees, and then returned to my stakeout.  At 8:49 a slightly larger flock finally flew in, doing large circles of the ball field area. I jumped out of the car and snapped flight photos, assuming they wouldn't stop again. Looking through these photos I can confirm some bohemians were present. But this time they alighted on a tall pine quite distant, adjacent to the baseball field (I snapped a photo of the tree in question later with a blue jay on it to give some reference--check the bluejay pic).  This was a small flock still--maybe 40 birds. But there were at least 4 bohemians mixed in. Got a few more photos and then the bohemians departed, leaving the cedar flock only. They never came down to the fruiting berries to eat, even though it was snowing and cold. I hung around until about 10:30 but only a small flock of CEWA ever showed up again. Not nearly the large flock numbers of 200+ people have been reporting.  Definitely a huge test of patience but super rewarding to get this dope lifer.

CG: A sentimental birding moment for me. I missed the RI goose last winter, the one that foraged on the athletic fields of my high school. I’ve developed a strange attachment to it because there was something melancholic yet powerful about the idea of a vagrant from Eurasia standing among native Canadas on the very fields I walked across as a scared teenager when I first came to the US.    All year I kept hearing the question “did you go see the RI goose?” and even while birding in SF I coincidentally ran into Chelsea from NJ who took the goose photographs at the school: https://ebird.org/checklist/S211528327    Finally seeing this goose I’ve grown to identify with, here in my new home in NY with friends, feels deeply comforting.

Arrived still in the dark to see one birder, Matt, already with his scope up. Did a few NYtimes games on my phone until it got slightly more reasonable of lighting conditions and joined him. Gorgeous view from up above the berm. Tons of dark shadow sleeping geese -- estimated at least a thousand by best guess.  Then the Where's Waldo game began as more light gave us more details on the birds. Over half were still sleeping. Scanned through the ones in the water many times as it would be most obvious there, but remained pretty sure it wasn't among them. Several trips to the car to refill coffee and add more layers of clothing, and the several more birders joined us.  At approximately 720ish, I caught a glimpse of white fringing on some wing feathers of a sleeping goose tucked in. I called it out and got everyone on it. Despite being almost entirely certain this HAD to be our tundra goose, I didn't want to post it to the Rhode Island groupme until it's head came untucked. And low and behold around 730, it did. I sent the alert out, the whole crew congratulated each other, and I believe Matt got back home in time for baseball.  Great to meet Danny and Ron. Super fun morning of sitting and watching the goose walk around, preen, swim, drink water, and take multiple naps.  Later in the morning I joined others closer down on the reservoir-edge berm. We watched it cozy up into a flock of sleeping canadas, and then I took my eyes off it for a moment, heard a commotion of a few geese flying, and completely lost it. it must've taken off right as I took my eyes off. Amazing bird and great way to celebrate the end of January recitals

11:20-1ish stationary skywatch by her majesty  then a loop of the park  chatted with madeleine.  sick day can't stop me from getting two new park birds and one Bronx bird    so rip to birdcast: it officially turned off on november 15 and we wont be graced with her presence again until March 1.  seemed like an overall big migration night though with many bluebirds, pipits, and songbirds reported all over the city.  initial plan was to celebrate being done with work by waking up at sunrise and doing morning flight at franz, then drive to pelham to meet up with rich and alyssa. but a fever intervened and i spent the night shivering, falling asleep at 4 and finally waking up at 1030 to a lot of FOMO from reports all over the city of big bird movement.    felt marginally better though, so i bundled up, got a smoothie and a sandwich and plopped down in the grass on the watch hill for a stationary 1:30 min watch.  enormously successful with one flyover pipit (picked up by merlin and then me moments later). wish i had gotten eyes on him because he sounded VERY close. would've loved a pic. N to S flight.  alyssa then posted a bluebird at pelham and i got very salty because my cold thwarted my target bird bluebird plans. it didn't help that merlin told me bluebird was my bird of the day.  but literally as i was sending her a screenshot of my BotD and complaining that i'd never see one at franz, a tuwuwuwU call came out of the sky to the W of me. i glanced down at merlin and it agreed with me: tuwuwuWU for sure.  incredibly, i got eyes and photos on a flock of 8 of them as they flew north over the NW woods of the park.  pretty quiet after that excitement. i thought bluebird was a county bird for me, but it turns out i saw one last year at pelham (where i also met hailey for the first time). but still a franz bird is just as good.    this songbird flight gave way to a slow but steady movement of raptors. many TUVU, red tailed hawks, and a bunch of extremely high up buteos I couldn't make out. I was also watching the CT group me where there were more reports of Golden Eagles drifting towards NY.    black vulture, broad winged hawk, bald eagle, golden eagle, and red-shouldered hawk were all the targets as my brain switched to raptor mode.    and lo and behold, a red-shouldered came over with a sharpie and a RTHA. beautiful orange underneath with black and white fringing to the wings and a lovely banded tail. i was worried i wouldn't recognize one if it came by, so i took a ton of pics just to be sure, but my instincts were right.    overall an amazing outcome for a late start day. welcome new franz birds 128 and 129: eastern bluebird and red-shouldered hawk <3

Checklist Comments: so after a grouse morning, the plan was to hit up some different spots that people had recently seen red-naped and williamson's sapsuckers.  The first stop was going to be Hartley Springs Campground where Alvin and Ellen had a pair on 04/04, but when I got there I saw it was a snow covered road and I wasn't about to brave it in my rental with no snow tires. The next option was Twin Lakes Campground, where Colin Danch had one on 04/14. It was going to be a long drive and I was a little bummed out that I have driven 35 minutes north already just to get to a closed road. But as I was driving south again, I noticed I was near the hotspot "Owens River Rd.--1 mile east of Hwy 395" which I recognized from Steve Glover and Darlene McNeil's trip report from a few years ago. I decided since it was on my way, I'd poke in quickly since they had Williamson's here years ago. Plus Grub Fay had reported one in January of this year. Popped in and within 15 minutes had a Williamsons pair drumming. Amazingly fortunate and felt really smiled upon by the universe. All that spreadsheet work paid off!  Lifer cassin's finch female was also here, along with tons of fun red crossbills, brown creepers, chickadees, MORE white-headed woodpeckers, and merlin even picked up an Evening Grosbeak, but I didn't see it so not listing it.

Which by my book is a win since I've been trying all year to put this place on the birding map. if more people are checking it out, more birds are gonna get seen. so altogether a dope morning.  a bit Fetid that I didn't get to see a clay colored tho.    oh yeah and one cool partial leucistic chipper :)

pretty confident with this ID. Empid flying around the treetops at the southern edge of ball fields in part of the recent empid invasion wave of migrants. Good alder habitat--nothing wet/shrubby around for willows.  faint eyering--not as pronounced as the leasts that I have been seeing around the park lately. chest not dark enough for a pewee. grayish and drab overall, not enough color for acadian/yellow-bellied. Felt good for Traill's.  i used a bit of playback to see if i could get a vocalization from it, but it stayed silent. about an hour later it reappeared, flew to a far canopy, and made VERY faint pip calls. Recorded via merlin and investigated at home on Raven Lite. The call notes, while very quiet, were bell-shaped (i.e. not a straight upwards "whit" like a willow). Compared to the frequency of some macauley library pip calls and noted that they both peaked at approx. the exact same frequency range: 3700hz.  Including a short, edited section of recording here where four pips can be heard at the following time stamps: 2.14, 4.56, 6.10, 8.40. The call at 6.10 is the loudest and most diagnostic i think.  Not great at these IDs, so please let me know if this feels not quite right!    UPDATE 05/29:  Switching all photos to Least Flycatcher, but keeping the pip calls on the Alder. Did not see the bird vocalizing, so not 100% sure it was the same bird as I had photographed slightly earlier. When I went back later in the afternoon, there were at least two empids up in the same treetops. Likely a Least and an Alder confusing me.

since i had missed my Vaux's Swift at bear divide earlier, i checked ebird for recent reports that were on the way from bear divide to ballona creek where i had to get that afternoon. Michael Klotz and Carli Wyllie had reported some at "Sepulveda Basin--East of Woodley Ave" on 4/16, so that became the next stop. Eyeballing the map, I thought the east basin close to the 405 would be the most likely spot, so I tried there first. TONS of swallows on the water, which I tried to photograph for quite awhile hoping to land a swift. But they were all foraging right on the water, whereas my gut was telling me a swift would prefer to be foraging high up in the air. After not turning up anything for about 30 minutes, I checked ebird once again and saw that a new report from Robert Thoren had just come in on 4/17 that there were two at the Lake Balboa hotspot on the other side of the park. I hightailed it over there, jumped out of the car and saw a MASSIVE flock of swallows circling above the parking lot. This seemed WAY more promising, as they were all up high. I ditched the camera for awhile and just stared up at different shapes, trying to remember what Matt told me last year when we were looking for a white throated swift when I asked him how he was able to tell apart a swift from a swallow: "swifts just look like swifts--not like swallows."  And boom. Something that looked like a swift. Smaller, no real protruding tail feathers, and all dark. Tracked it for awhile in bins and then switched to camera and got some idable shots. Great last lifer for the trip

quick drive around looking for pinyon jays/mountain bluebirds  More:  Pinyon Jay search continued with a slow drive down Old Sherwin Grade Road, and eventually up to Swall Meadows. Checklist Comments: all morning search for Ms. wandering tattler  success in the final hour right before island packer.  More details:  Started at the jetty across from Island Packer lot. Wasn't having a ton of luck there, so drove to the other side of the creek mouth to scope from there, where I got absolutely nailed by a wave. Had to go to CVS to get lens cleaner to clean my scope, nocs, and glasses. Came back to the north side and continued scoping from safer locations away from waves. Still no luck with Tattler. Drove back to the south side of the creek mouth and checked the "surfers knoll" area, then back to the initial scoping spot across from Island Packers. There was a surfing competition going on, and one of the announcements was loud enough to scare up a flock of shorebirds previously tucked away in the rocky jetty. Out of this mostly white-wing striped crowd (willet, surfbird, turnstone, peep), there was one all dark-winged individual that I immediately clocked and stayed on with nocs. It flew across the beach in front of me and landed on the north shoreline, a little before the start of the jetty. I checked my sibley app and found that indeed the tattler had all dark wings, so sprinted up the beach with my scope and found the tattler blended in perfectly with the rocks. Was an awesome chase day with a skin-of-my-teeth rewarding ending as I had to go check in with the Island Packers boat 15 minutes later.

Checklist Comments: absolutely stellar morning at Franz.  started at my usual spot mid park where it was a bit quiet and dark still. but heard what sounded like a great crested coming from the ball fields to the south. realized I never really check the tree line from INSIDE the ball fields, and have seen people running their dogs in there, so went to go check it out.  best decision of the day. immediately started hearing tons of warbler song, and the sun was hitting these southwest trees in full getting the bugs really active.  btgreen, mag, BTblue, yellow, and redstart were all quite readily found, a long with a vocal RBGR  biggest shocker came with a Wilson's warbler tucked deep in the lower branches. my first for the Bronx and a first of the year for me. huge win.  swallows came next with a glance at a tree swallow and good looks at a barn swallow.  hung around for an hour or so before exploring the rest of the park, which yielded some really close views of feeding Blackpolls in a reddish purple beech tree (thanks Jules)  gb heron flyover really cinched the morning.  wanted ovenbird and a thrush on the way out, so walked the Walton slopes and got my patch Swainsons :)))  most fire morning of the Franz season

Walked along the southern property line and found a mixed flock of songbirds similar to the one I had the previous day: chickadees, nuthatches, creepers, titmice, and notably another single blue-headed vireo. Observation Details: with a mixed foraging flock of chickadees, kinglets, and a pine warbler. blue head and white spectacles. seen briefly before it moved past
Checklist Comments: Arrived at about 7:15am to start my thanksgiving red cockaded woodpecker search. Parked at the trailhead marked Lipford Path and walked clockwise around the loop. Very quiet at first. On the northwest corner of the loop in the more woodsy park there was a large mixed flock of passerines whose presence was made known by the trumpeting of a bunch of boisterous chickadees. They were outdone in intensity however by the golden crowned kinglets who were making an equally noisy racket. Tucked away amongst these little fellows however were two oddities: a brief appearance by a blue-headed vireo--only seen for a moment but enough to spot the blue head and white spectacles. Was immediately distracted by an almost neon yellow bird that shot past in the background of my binoculars. After a bit of searching through more kinglets, the yellow bird appeared again to show itself as a pine warbler. A larger bird than all the nearby kinglets, with a nice olive back and subtle facial marks contrasting its lemondrop belly.    After the passerine flock passed, it was back to searching for red-cockaded. The northern edge of the loop was quiet, other than a few gunshots from hunters and dogs howling. A pileated flew by in a brief shock of contrasting red, black, and white, which brought the woodpecker total up to 3 seen (downy, hairy, pileated) and two heard (red-bellied, flicker). But still no cockaded. As I turned south and began walking down the eastern edge of the loop I resigned myself to taking a coffee/food break and returning to search for the cockaded later. I sped up my walk a bit but paused when a group of white-throated sparrows and other passerines started making a racket again. That's when I started hearing the tapping of beaks on trees and saw a flurry of woodpecker-like movement in the pine treetops. A group of 5-6 red cockaded woodpeckers with bright white cheeks, an absence of black eye streaks, and dirty gray spotting down the flanks flew in and foraged in the north-east corner of the loop for almost an hour while I took very far away distant photos.    Hunger finally got to me and I decided to return to the car, but on the last leg of the loop I encountered a 2nd group of red-cockaded, with some even close enough to take decent photos of.    A huge success with two life birds for me--didn't even mention the brown-headed nuthatches. But they're dope too.

absolutely stellar morning at Franz.  started at my usual spot mid park where it was a bit quiet and dark still. but heard what sounded like a great crested coming from the ball fields to the south. realized I never really check the tree line from INSIDE the ball fields, and have seen people running their dogs in there, so went to go check it out.  best decision of the day. immediately started hearing tons of warbler song, and the sun was hitting these southwest trees in full getting the bugs really active.  btgreen, mag, BTblue, yellow, and redstart were all quite readily found, a long with a vocal RBGR  biggest shocker came with a Wilson's warbler tucked deep in the lower branches. my first for the Bronx and a first of the year for me. huge win.  swallows came next with a glance at a tree swallow and good looks at a barn swallow.  hung around for an hour or so before exploring the rest of the park, which yielded some really close views of feeding Blackpolls in a reddish purple beech tree (thanks Jules)  gb heron flyover really cinched the morning.  wanted ovenbird and a thrush on the way out, so walked the Walton slopes and got my patch Swainsons :)))  most fire morning of the Franz season

Checklist Comments: I have no words right now    Alright here's more words now that I'm back in NYC.  Second stop here. First one on the way up was fruitless. I emailed Bob Steele the night before and asked him for some details on whereabouts he finds the Pinyon Jays since he's reported them multiple times recently. He responded RIGHT away but somehow I didn't see it til after I stopped here. His response was:  "Freeman Canyon goes west on Highway 178 from Highway 14. The best place for PIJAs is near the summit at Walker Pass. You can park anywhere on both sides of the road at the pass. We last had them by walking north on the Pacific Crest Trail from the pass about half a mile. That said, they range widely in the area. Another good spot to try is the campground a short distance west from the pass (Walker Pass Campground). They are best found first by hearing them. It’s breeding season so there aren’t the large flocks we usually see at other times of the year. The Pacific Crest Trail goes south from the campground towards an area of high pinyon pine density that usually has some nesting birds."    So now for my anecdote:  At this point I had searched Tuff Campgrounds, Swall Meadows, the Rock Creek Trail, and White Mountain 3 consecutive days for over 10 hours for pinyon jays with no luck and had decided that I was just not going to see them on this trip. Heartbreaking I know. But as I was driving back south towards Lancaster, I figured why the hell not stop one more time at Walker Pass campgroudns to see if I could land them. I took a lot of courage from Joan Campbell's 3/22 checklist about how they parked and listened, walked up the trail, and then had them flyover.  So what's another 20 minute detour off of 395 I thought.    So im rounding the hairpin ass turn at 35.669536, -118.035683 and a blue bird with a long thick beak and a fanned out tail flies over my car as i'm going 15 mph and i yell out loud in my car "what the actual f@#$ was that", knowing that it was my jay. It was flying north to south, so I knew it could be seen passing the campground momentarily. Let me tell you i SPED to the campground, drove up the highest point of it, leapt out of the car and heard a flock of about 5 of them flying past. I photographed them as quickly as I could in blurry speed shots, then saw them perch in a distant dead tree. I raced back to the car to grab my scope, leaving a trail of granola bar wrappers and dirty clothes as I scrambled to set up the tripod legs and looked at they were already gone.  I walked back to the car to clean up my clothes and trash strewn across the parking lot, took a deep breath and turned back just in time to see my scope topple over--I hadn't properly set up the tripod.  Took some battle scars on the eyecup, but overall wasn't cracked out damaged optically as far as I could tell.    Decided to walk the trail south a ways to about here:  35.661612, -118.037509  That's when bigger flocks of them started to call out and appear. Stayed in that general area for about an hour and had about 3 full flock passes going by north to south and then back again.    What an insane end to the pinyon jay saga.  One of the craziest bird seeking experiences of my life.

Location: Big Pine Canyon--Glacier Lodge and campgrounds
Checklist Comments: incredible spot. tons of notes to say later  okay so first things first i was almost not going to drive to mono county on this trip. I was getting cold feet back in santa barbara about rushing things, not taking my time, long drive etc. but i'm SO glad i did even if just for this checklist. This campground was an absolutely bombshell of lifers and surprises. Booming sooty grouse, american DIPPER!!! which i wasn't even thinking I'd see this trip. And then the surprise white-headed woodpcekr legitimately changed the course of the end of my trip, as I was planning on driving up to chilao campgrounds back in LA for this. The sapsucker was incredible. The temperature was amazing. One of my favorite checklists from the whole trip was right here.

Funny enough, this is basically where I camped the night before without really realizing it. So after so much success during the early morning, and riding high from my williamsons find, I wanted to try for Pinyon Jays again (having spent a lot of the previous afternoon on White Mountain listening for them).  The first stop was above Tuff Campgrounds on this dirt roads where Matt James had recently reported them on a few days in a row. No sign of them, but better looks at a Cassin's Finch and some Violet-green Swallows were a nice treat. Another unexpected treat was a gull call which made me look up in time to get some pics of a flock of California Gulls going over    NOTE:  If you're reading this and thinking of camping at Tuff Campgrounds, the road in was closed when I tried it the night before on April 14.

Location: Grand Marais RV Park and Campground
Checklist Comments: lots of Bohemian Waxwing details later  okay so this was by far my longest stakeout. tried the previous afternoon and not a single waxwing appeared from 12:30-sunset.  day two i showed up in the morning and it was dead silent for about an hour. Was parked by the bathrooms/boats/baseball field area by the coke machine.  At 8:09am a small flock of waxwings flew over but did not stop. They flew in from the south and headed north towards the west side of Grand Marais. Then about 15 minutes later with the windows down I heard a single bird making a trilling call in the pines near the baseball field. I drove around the RV park looking for the single bird but couldn't find him, did a lap of the west side neighborhood to check the fruiting trees, and then returned to my stakeout.  At 8:49 a slightly larger flock finally flew in, doing large circles of the ball field area. I jumped out of the car and snapped flight photos, assuming they wouldn't stop again. Looking through these photos I can confirm some bohemians were present. But this time they alighted on a tall pine quite distant, adjacent to the baseball field (I snapped a photo of the tree in question later with a blue jay on it to give some reference--check the bluejay pic).  This was a small flock still--maybe 40 birds. But there were at least 4 bohemians mixed in. Got a few more photos and then the bohemians departed, leaving the cedar flock only. They never came down to the fruiting berries to eat, even though it was snowing and cold. I hung around until about 10:30 but only a small flock of CEWA ever showed up again. Not nearly the large flock numbers of 200+ people have been reporting.  Definitely a huge test of patience but super rewarding to get this dope lifer.

CG: A sentimental birding moment for me. I missed the RI goose last winter, the one that foraged on the athletic fields of my high school. I’ve developed a strange attachment to it because there was something melancholic yet powerful about the idea of a vagrant from Eurasia standing among native Canadas on the very fields I walked across as a scared teenager when I first came to the US.    All year I kept hearing the question “did you go see the RI goose?” and even while birding in SF I coincidentally ran into Chelsea from NJ who took the goose photographs at the school: https://ebird.org/checklist/S211528327    Finally seeing this goose I’ve grown to identify with, here in my new home in NY with friends, feels deeply comforting.

Arrived still in the dark to see one birder, Matt, already with his scope up. Did a few NYtimes games on my phone until it got slightly more reasonable of lighting conditions and joined him. Gorgeous view from up above the berm. Tons of dark shadow sleeping geese -- estimated at least a thousand by best guess.  Then the Where's Waldo game began as more light gave us more details on the birds. Over half were still sleeping. Scanned through the ones in the water many times as it would be most obvious there, but remained pretty sure it wasn't among them. Several trips to the car to refill coffee and add more layers of clothing, and the several more birders joined us.  At approximately 720ish, I caught a glimpse of white fringing on some wing feathers of a sleeping goose tucked in. I called it out and got everyone on it. Despite being almost entirely certain this HAD to be our tundra goose, I didn't want to post it to the Rhode Island groupme until it's head came untucked. And low and behold around 730, it did. I sent the alert out, the whole crew congratulated each other, and I believe Matt got back home in time for baseball.  Great to meet Danny and Ron. We watched it cozy up into a flock of sleeping canadas, and then I took my eyes off it for a moment, heard a commotion of a few geese flying, and completely lost it. it must've taken off right as I took my eyes off. incredibly risky chase for a incredibly rare bird.  checked the Wilbur avenue fields where it was seen in the late afternoon of January 13 first. Was still dark out but could tell there were no roosting birds--which makes sense--i would prefer water as well.  Next stop was a pin on Salem Street parallel to the Batten Kill river. Through the houses I could see there was a decent number 40+ geese on the ice. Sent out a quick message on discord that geese were present. But viewing conditions were hard as the geese were further west of the pin and it was on a residential street. After a few attempts at scoping the geese in between houses (and a dirty look from a woman in her kitchen), I decided to hustle over to the opposite side of the river to try a different vantage point. Drove a little too fast through sleepy Greenwich.  Saw the name Rock Street and headed down that way to the PERFECT vantage point. And lo and behold there were about 150 more geese bathing on the north side of the river that was previously unviewable from the Salem pin. I excitedly started scanning and didn't see any non-canada at first. No yellow/orange bills poked out through the sea of black/white/and gray. And then boom -- noticed an all gray head that didn't match the  CANG. stayed on it while it faced away from me, then watched it turn and cinched the ID with the black/orange bill. Immediately skipped a heartbeat, digiscoped a shot and sent the pic and co-ords to discord at 7:18am.  I stayed for roughly two more hours and watched it swim, feed, drink water, get spooked by eagles, climb up on the ice, do a few wing flaps, and take about a 35 minute nap.  Was joined soon after finding it by Barbara Mansell, Debbie van Zyl, and Zach Shaoul. Lovely time chatting with them and bonding over this amazing bird, and later with Bob Proniewych from Nassau county.  Back in the city by 1pm and ready for a nap.

Was going to start using playback and then was like "what am i doing" so    drove back down and got coffee at Brewed Awakenings (thanks for being open at 5). Unsatisfied with my 5 hours of pinyon jay searching the previous day, I decided to give it another morning.   The itinerary at this point was to drive back to Lancaster today, stopping along the way, and then wake up on Thursday to find a LeConte's thrasher before driving into LA to return my car that afternoon. So what basically I had a full day to kill, minus the 3.5 hour drive to Lancaster.  Basically repeated the previous day's path--started at Cedar Flats photographing some Junipers, went up to Grandview Campground (where I had my lifer Gray Flycatcher), took an extended stop at the Vista View, then up to Bristlecone for a brief walk around. I stopped every quarter mile or so on the road to listen for Pinyon Jays on the way up and the way down. Nothing doing. Cool flyby Clarks at Vista View. But overall a tough strike out on Jays.

On the way to mono county decided to stop over here for an initial check for Pinyon Jays based on Andrew Hood and Stephanie Levins's 03/29 checklist. Really pretty area, but no sign of jays. I asked a local camper if a big group of noisy blue jays had been noticed and he said no, just a single blue jay (that I assumed was the cali scrub jay i had just seen).  Little did I know this campground would prove fruitful on my way back several days later >:)

I have no words right now    Alright here's more words now that I'm back in NYC.  Second stop here. First one on the way up was fruitless. I emailed Bob Steele the night before and asked him for some details on whereabouts he finds the Pinyon Jays since he's reported them multiple times recently. He responded RIGHT away but somehow I didn't see it til after I stopped here. His response was:  "Freeman Canyon goes west on Highway 178 from Highway 14. The best place for PIJAs is near the summit at Walker Pass. You can park anywhere on both sides of the road at the pass. We last had them by walking north on the Pacific Crest Trail from the pass about half a mile. That said, they range widely in the area. Another good spot to try is the campground a short distance west from the pass (Walker Pass Campground). They are best found first by hearing them. It’s breeding season so there aren’t the large flocks we usually see at other times of the year. The Pacific Crest Trail goes south from the campground towards an area of high pinyon pine density that usually has some nesting birds."    So now for my anecdote:  At this point I had searched Tuff Campgrounds, Swall Meadows, the Rock Creek Trail, and White Mountain 3 consecutive days for over 10 hours for pinyon jays with no luck and had decided that I was just not going to see them on this trip. Heartbreaking I know. But as I was driving back south towards Lancaster, I figured why the hell not stop one more time at Walker Pass campgroudns to see if I could land them. I took a lot of courage from Joan Campbell's 3/22 checklist about how they parked and listened, walked up the trail, and then had them flyover.  So what's another 20 minute detour off of 395 I thought.    So im rounding the hairpin ass turn at 35.669536, -118.035683 and a blue bird with a long thick beak and a fanned out tail flies over my car as i'm going 15 mph and i yell out loud in my car "what the actual f@#$ was that", knowing that it was my jay. It was flying north to south, so I knew it could be seen passing the campground momentarily. Let me tell you i SPED to the campground, drove up the highest point of it, leapt out of the car and heard a flock of about 5 of them flying past. I photographed them as quickly as I could in blurry speed shots, then saw them perch in a distant dead tree. I raced back to the car to grab my scope, leaving a trail of granola bar wrappers and dirty clothes as I scrambled to set up the tripod legs and looked at they were already gone.  I walked back to the car to clean up my clothes and trash strewn across the parking lot, took a deep breath and turned back just in time to see my scope topple over--I hadn't properly set up the tripod.  Took some battle scars on the eyecup, but overall wasn't cracked out damaged optically as far as I could tell.    Decided to walk the trail south a ways to about here:  35.661612, -118.037509  That's when bigger flocks of them started to call out and appear. Stayed in that general area for about an hour and had about 3 full flock passes going by north to south and then back again.    What an insane end to the pinyon jay saga.  One of the craziest bird seeking experiences of my life.

11:20-1ish stationary skywatch by her majesty  then a loop of the park  chatted with madeleine.  sick day can't stop me from getting two new park birds and one Bronx bird    so rip to birdcast: it officially turned off on november 15 and we wont be graced with her presence again until March 1.  seemed like an overall big migration night though with many bluebirds, pipits, and songbirds reported all over the city.  initial plan was to celebrate being done with work by waking up at sunrise and doing morning flight at franz, then drive to pelham to meet up with rich and alyssa. but a fever intervened and i spent the night shivering, falling asleep at 4 and finally waking up at 1030 to a lot of FOMO from reports all over the city of big bird movement.    felt marginally better though, so i bundled up, got a smoothie and a sandwich and plopped down in the grass on the watch hill for a stationary 1:30 min watch.  enormously successful with one flyover pipit (picked up by merlin and then me moments later). wish i had gotten eyes on him because he sounded VERY close. would've loved a pic. N to S flight.  alyssa then posted a bluebird at pelham and i got very salty because my cold thwarted my target bird bluebird plans. it didn't help that merlin told me bluebird was my bird of the day.  but literally as i was sending her a screenshot of my BotD and complaining that i'd never see one at franz, a tuwuwuwU call came out of the sky to the W of me. i glanced down at merlin and it agreed with me: tuwuwuWU for sure.  incredibly, i got eyes and photos on a flock of 8 of them as they flew north over the NW woods of the park.  pretty quiet after that excitement. i thought bluebird was a county bird for me, but it turns out i saw one last year at pelham (where i also met hailey for the first time). but still a franz bird is just as good.    this songbird flight gave way to a slow but steady movement of raptors. many TUVU, red tailed hawks, and a bunch of extremely high up buteos I couldn't make out. I was also watching the CT group me where there were more reports of Golden Eagles drifting towards NY.    black vulture, broad winged hawk, bald eagle, golden eagle, and red-shouldered hawk were all the targets as my brain switched to raptor mode.    and lo and behold, a red-shouldered came over with a sharpie and a RTHA. beautiful orange underneath with black and white fringing to the wings and a lovely banded tail. i was worried i wouldn't recognize one if it came by, so i took a ton of pics just to be sure, but my instincts were right.    overall an amazing outcome for a late start day. welcome new franz birds 128 and 129: eastern bluebird and red-shouldered hawk <3

Location: Grand Marais RV Park and Campground
Checklist Comments: lots of Bohemian Waxwing details later  okay so this was by far my longest stakeout. tried the previous afternoon and not a single waxwing appeared from 12:30-sunset.  day two i showed up in the morning and it was dead silent for about an hour. Was parked by the bathrooms/boats/baseball field area by the coke machine.  At 8:09am a small flock of waxwings flew over but did not stop. They flew in from the south and headed north towards the west side of Grand Marais. Then about 15 minutes later with the windows down I heard a single bird making a trilling call in the pines near the baseball field. I drove around the RV park looking for the single bird but couldn't find him, did a lap of the west side neighborhood to check the fruiting trees, and then returned to my stakeout.  At 8:49 a slightly larger flock finally flew in, doing large circles of the ball field area. I jumped out of the car and snapped flight photos, assuming they wouldn't stop again. Looking through these photos I can confirm some bohemians were present. But this time they alighted on a tall pine quite distant, adjacent to the baseball field (I snapped a photo of the tree in question later with a blue jay on it to give some reference--check the bluejay pic).  This was a small flock still--maybe 40 birds. But there were at least 4 bohemians mixed in. Got a few more photos and then the bohemians departed, leaving the cedar flock only. They never came down to the fruiting berries to eat, even though it was snowing and cold. I hung around until about 10:30 but only a small flock of CEWA ever showed up again. Not nearly the large flock numbers of 200+ people have been reporting.  Definitely a huge test of patience but super rewarding to get this dope lifer.

Wanted to come back to Constance Darden trail after driving by the afternoon before. Was in search of red-cockaded woodpeckers. Walked along the southern property line and found a mixed flock of songbirds similar to the one I had the previous day: chickadees, nuthatches, creepers, titmice, and notably another single blue-headed vireo.  Things quieted down once I got back to the main trail and were completely silent while I staked out the observation deck for 30 minutes or so. No cockaded woodpeckers.  Also, the red-shouldered hawk was seen along the road on the way in.

Arrived at about 7:15am to start my thanksgiving red cockaded woodpecker search. Parked at the trailhead marked Lipford Path and walked clockwise around the loop. Very quiet at first. On the northwest corner of the loop in the more woodsy park there was a large mixed flock of passerines whose presence was made known by the trumpeting of a bunch of boisterous chickadees. They were outdone in intensity however by the golden crowned kinglets who were making an equally noisy racket. Tucked away amongst these little fellows however were two oddities: a brief appearance by a blue-headed vireo--only seen for a moment but enough to spot the blue head and white spectacles. Was immediately distracted by an almost neon yellow bird that shot past in the background of my binoculars. After a bit of searching through more kinglets, the yellow bird appeared again to show itself as a pine warbler. A larger bird than all the nearby kinglets, with a nice olive back and subtle facial marks contrasting its lemondrop belly.    After the passerine flock passed, it was back to searching for red-cockaded. The northern edge of the loop was quiet, other than a few gunshots from hunters and dogs howling. A pileated flew by in a brief shock of contrasting red, black, and white, which brought the woodpecker total up to 3 seen (downy, hairy, pileated) and two heard (red-bellied, flicker). But still no cockaded. As I turned south and began walking down the eastern edge of the loop I resigned myself to taking a coffee/food break and returning to search for the cockaded later. I sped up my walk a bit but paused when a group of white-throated sparrows and other passerines started making a racket again. That's when I started hearing the tapping of beaks on trees and saw a flurry of woodpecker-like movement in the pine treetops. A group of 5-6 red cockaded woodpeckers with bright white cheeks, an absence of black eye streaks, and dirty gray spotting down the flanks flew in and foraged in the north-east corner of the loop for almost an hour while I took very far away distant photos.    Hunger finally got to me and I decided to return to the car, but on the last leg of the loop I encountered a 2nd group of red-cockaded, with some even close enough to take decent photos of.    A huge success with two life birds for me--didn't even mention the brown-headed nuthatches. But they're dope too.

Returned to the same trail from 11/23/2023, but this time entered at the more eastern end of the loop and returned to the general location of the previous day's red-cockaded woodpeckers. Was there for about 30 minutes before hearing gentle tapping high up in the trees and a group of RCWO foraged their way into view. A lone downy woodpecker also tried to fake me out into thinking there was a RCWO 2 feet from me.  Another lemondrop yellow pine warbler showed up at one point. And a few bald eagles flew overhead (or possibly the same one circling). Lots of hunting gunshots--sort of eerie. The RCWO brought a nice calming feeling though.

all morning search for Ms. wandering tattler  success in the final hour right before island packer.  More details:  Started at the jetty across from Island Packer lot. Wasn't having a ton of luck there, so drove to the other side of the creek mouth to scope from there, where I got absolutely nailed by a wave. Had to go to CVS to get lens cleaner to clean my scope, nocs, and glasses. Came back to the north side and continued scoping from safer locations away from waves. Still no luck with Tattler. Drove back to the south side of the creek mouth and checked the "surfers knoll" area, then back to the initial scoping spot across from Island Packers. There was a surfing competition going on, and one of the announcements was loud enough to scare up a flock of shorebirds previously tucked away in the rocky jetty. Out of this mostly white-wing striped crowd (willet, surfbird, turnstone, peep), there was one all dark-winged individual that I immediately clocked and stayed on with nocs. It flew across the beach in front of me and landed on the north shoreline, a little before the start of the jetty. I checked my sibley app and found that indeed the tattler had all dark wings, so sprinted up the beach with my scope and found the tattler blended in perfectly with the rocks. Was an awesome chase day with a skin-of-my-teeth rewarding ending as I had to go check in with the Island Packers boat 15 minutes later.

incredibly risky chase for a incredibly rare bird.  checked the Wilbur avenue fields where it was seen in the late afternoon of January 13 first. Was still dark out but could tell there were no roosting birds--which makes sense--i would prefer water as well.  Next stop was a pin on Salem Street parallel to the Batten Kill river. Through the houses I could see there was a decent number 40+ geese on the ice. Sent out a quick message on discord that geese were present. But viewing conditions were hard as the geese were further west of the pin and it was on a residential street. After a few attempts at scoping the geese in between houses (and a dirty look from a woman in her kitchen), I decided to hustle over to the opposite side of the river to try a different vantage point. Drove a little too fast through sleepy Greenwich.  Saw the name Rock Street and headed down that way to the PERFECT vantage point. And lo and behold there were about 150 more geese bathing on the north side of the river that was previously unviewable from the Salem pin. I excitedly started scanning and didn't see any non-canada at first. No yellow/orange bills poked out through the sea of black/white/and gray. And then boom -- noticed an all gray head that didn't match the  CANG. stayed on it while it faced away from me, then watched it turn and cinched the ID with the black/orange bill. Immediately skipped a heartbeat, digiscoped a shot and sent the pic and co-ords to discord at 7:18am.  I stayed for roughly two more hours and watched it swim, feed, drink water, get spooked by eagles, climb up on the ice, do a few wing flaps, and take about a 35 minute nap.  Was joined soon after finding it by Barbara Mansell, Debbie van Zyl, and Zach Shaoul. Lovely time chatting with them and bonding over this amazing bird, and later with Bob Proniewych from Nassau county.  Back in the city by 1pm and ready for a nap.

11:20-1ish stationary skywatch by her majesty  then a loop of the park  chatted with madeleine.  sick day can't stop me from getting two new park birds and one Bronx bird    so rip to birdcast: it officially turned off on november 15 and we wont be graced with her presence again until March 1.  seemed like an overall big migration night though with many bluebirds, pipits, and songbirds reported all over the city.  initial plan was to celebrate being done with work by waking up at sunrise and doing morning flight at franz, then drive to pelham to meet up with rich and alyssa. but a fever intervened and i spent the night shivering, falling asleep at 4 and finally waking up at 1030 to a lot of FOMO from reports all over the city of big bird movement.    felt marginally better though, so i bundled up, got a smoothie and a sandwich and plopped down in the grass on the watch hill for a stationary 1:30 min watch.  enormously successful with one flyover pipit (picked up by merlin and then me moments later). wish i had gotten eyes on him because he sounded VERY close. would've loved a pic. N to S flight.  alyssa then posted a bluebird at pelham and i got very salty because my cold thwarted my target bird bluebird plans. it didn't help that merlin told me bluebird was my bird of the day.  but literally as i was sending her a screenshot of my BotD and complaining that i'd never see one at franz, a tuwuwuwU call came out of the sky to the W of me. i glanced down at merlin and it agreed with me: tuwuwuWU for sure.  incredibly, i got eyes and photos on a flock of 8 of them as they flew north over the NW woods of the park.  pretty quiet after that excitement. i thought bluebird was a county bird for me, but it turns out i saw one last year at pelham (where i also met hailey for the first time). but still a franz bird is just as good.    this songbird flight gave way to a slow but steady movement of raptors. many TUVU, red tailed hawks, and a bunch of extremely high up buteos I couldn't make out. I was also watching the CT group me where there were more reports of Golden Eagles drifting towards NY.    black vulture, broad winged hawk, bald eagle, golden eagle, and red-shouldered hawk were all the targets as my brain switched to raptor mode.    and lo and behold, a red-shouldered came over with a sharpie and a RTHA. beautiful orange underneath with black and white fringing to the wings and a lovely banded tail. i was worried i wouldn't recognize one if it came by, so i took a ton of pics just to be sure, but my instincts were right.    overall an amazing outcome for a late start day. welcome new franz birds 128 and 129: eastern bluebird and red-shouldered hawk <3

first big target bird of the trip.  parked at the airboat tour parking lot and began by checking the massive tree full of fish crow and grackles above the ramp. no cowbirds. walked north up the street and saw a few more grackle in between the houses. walked back south on the other side and got side tracked by egrets and herons.  then did a walk out to the west most road and saw my first female BH cowbird. seemed like a promising sign.  walked south from the airboat lot and found a tree with at least 6 roosting cowbirds in it. did a careful check of each but all had dark eyes and similar shape/beak shape. there were a lot of tangled nooks and crannies though, so I felt like it was possible I had missed some. chatted with a local and then walked back up to the parking area to check the big boat ramp tree. still no cowbirds.  walked BACK out to the west most road and found another small roost of cowbirds and grackles. most of the brown headed were all perched and not moving, but one was jumping from branch to branch and caught my eye. got enough of a peak at the face to see something was different with its eye. immediately grabbed camera and snapped some pics to reveal a red iris with a black pupil suspended in the middle.  glorious feeling. called Matt to tell him about it.  took a few more pics and then dipped cuz I thought everyone was probably sick of me walking through their neighborhood.  fun first lifer :)

day long excursion to Sandy hook. targets were Whimbrel, American golden plover, and Philadelphia vireo.  not a huge day for passerines. overcast, except for around 2-4. hot then.  tide was still quite hi when I arrived at 12pm. spermcetti cove had black bellied plovers, SEPL, RUTU, but all distant.  explored north end mudflats next where tide was starting to recede. very few shorebirds but immense tern colony. sure to have been roseates mixed in with common but couldn't pick any out.  stayed until around 4pm, then walked the beach south down to the North Beach parking lot. eider was just offshore there, a long with a few piping plovers.  made another pass at sperm cove, this time with much of the mudflats exposed. more AMOY and BBPL now but no good American golden candidates.  went back to North end mudflats right around 530 and found two Whimbrel sitting right in the main leftover puddle on the flats. took most of my photos there and then watched them takeoff. they then flew back in, this time with 4 more, and did several aerial passes of the flats doing flight calls. pretty spectacular to watch. briefly touched down nearby for a few more photos and then left the area just before sunset.  successful and movie-esque day!

Location: Grand Marais RV Park and Campground
Checklist Comments: lots of Bohemian Waxwing details later  okay so this was by far my longest stakeout. tried the previous afternoon and not a single waxwing appeared from 12:30-sunset.  day two i showed up in the morning and it was dead silent for about an hour. Was parked by the bathrooms/boats/baseball field area by the coke machine.  At 8:09am a small flock of waxwings flew over but did not stop. They flew in from the south and headed north towards the west side of Grand Marais. Then about 15 minutes later with the windows down I heard a single bird making a trilling call in the pines near the baseball field. I drove around the RV park looking for the single bird but couldn't find him, did a lap of the west side neighborhood to check the fruiting trees, and then returned to my stakeout.  At 8:49 a slightly larger flock finally flew in, doing large circles of the ball field area. I jumped out of the car and snapped flight photos, assuming they wouldn't stop again. Looking through these photos I can confirm some bohemians were present. But this time they alighted on a tall pine quite distant, adjacent to the baseball field (I snapped a photo of the tree in question later with a blue jay on it to give some reference--check the bluejay pic).  This was a small flock still--maybe 40 birds. But there were at least 4 bohemians mixed in. Got a few more photos and then the bohemians departed, leaving the cedar flock only. They never came down to the fruiting berries to eat, even though it was snowing and cold. I hung around until about 10:30 but only a small flock of CEWA ever showed up again. Not nearly the large flock numbers of 200+ people have been reporting.  Definitely a huge test of patience but super rewarding to get this dope lifer.

all day on the mountain checklist. details of notable birds and where they were seen in list. skill checked by pinyon jays.  chuck and Jenn motorcycle broz nice to meet ya    More notes:  I was cranky from my earlier pinyon jay search on the west side of highway 395, so why not spend the rest of the day looking over the entirety of White Mountain for pinyon jays?  This checklist is kind of all encompassing of White Mountain. Started at the flats off the highway, continued up to the grandview campground where I finally saw a mountain bluebird undeniably, then up to the bristlecone pine forest where I had my socks blown off by those trees. Unexpectedly ran into more Williamsons Sapsuckers up there which was a treat. But no Pinyon Jays, despite even playing their call a bit from my car speakers. The other target was a Clark's Nutcracker, which was beginning to feel like a no go, but finally got it on the dirt road past the bristle forest on my way back down.

Was going to start using playback and then was like "what am i doing" so    drove back down and got coffee at Brewed Awakenings (thanks for being open at 5). Unsatisfied with my 5 hours of pinyon jay searching the previous day, I decided to give it another morning.   The itinerary at this point was to drive back to Lancaster today, stopping along the way, and then wake up on Thursday to find a LeConte's thrasher before driving into LA to return my car that afternoon. So what basically I had a full day to kill, minus the 3.5 hour drive to Lancaster.  Basically repeated the previous day's path--started at Cedar Flats photographing some Junipers, went up to Grandview Campground (where I had my lifer Gray Flycatcher), took an extended stop at the Vista View, then up to Bristlecone for a brief walk around. I stopped every quarter mile or so on the road to listen for Pinyon Jays on the way up and the way down. Nothing doing. Cool flyby Clarks at Vista View. But overall a tough strike out on Jays.

I have no words right now    Alright here's more words now that I'm back in NYC.  Second stop here. First one on the way up was fruitless. I emailed Bob Steele the night before and asked him for some details on whereabouts he finds the Pinyon Jays since he's reported them multiple times recently. He responded RIGHT away but somehow I didn't see it til after I stopped here. His response was:  "Freeman Canyon goes west on Highway 178 from Highway 14. The best place for PIJAs is near the summit at Walker Pass. You can park anywhere on both sides of the road at the pass. We last had them by walking north on the Pacific Crest Trail from the pass about half a mile. That said, they range widely in the area. Another good spot to try is the campground a short distance west from the pass (Walker Pass Campground). They are best found first by hearing them. It’s breeding season so there aren’t the large flocks we usually see at other times of the year. The Pacific Crest Trail goes south from the campground towards an area of high pinyon pine density that usually has some nesting birds."    So now for my anecdote:  At this point I had searched Tuff Campgrounds, Swall Meadows, the Rock Creek Trail, and White Mountain 3 consecutive days for over 10 hours for pinyon jays with no luck and had decided that I was just not going to see them on this trip. Heartbreaking I know. But as I was driving back south towards Lancaster, I figured why the hell not stop one more time at Walker Pass campgroudns to see if I could land them. I took a lot of courage from Joan Campbell's 3/22 checklist about how they parked and listened, walked up the trail, and then had them flyover.  So what's another 20 minute detour off of 395 I thought.    So im rounding the hairpin ass turn at 35.669536, -118.035683 and a blue bird with a long thick beak and a fanned out tail flies over my car as i'm going 15 mph and i yell out loud in my car "what the actual f@#$ was that", knowing that it was my jay. It was flying north to south, so I knew it could be seen passing the campground momentarily. Let me tell you i SPED to the campground, drove up the highest point of it, leapt out of the car and heard a flock of about 5 of them flying past. I photographed them as quickly as I could in blurry speed shots, then saw them perch in a distant dead tree. I raced back to the car to grab my scope, leaving a trail of granola bar wrappers and dirty clothes as I scrambled to set up the tripod legs and looked at they were already gone.  I walked back to the car to clean up my clothes and trash strewn across the parking lot, took a deep breath and turned back just in time to see my scope topple over--I hadn't properly set up the tripod.  Took some battle scars on the eyecup, but overall wasn't cracked out damaged optically as far as I could tell.    Decided to walk the trail south a ways to about here:  35.661612, -118.037509  That's when bigger flocks of them started to call out and appear. Stayed in that general area for about an hour and had about 3 full flock passes going by north to south and then back again.    What an insane end to the pinyon jay saga.  One of the craziest bird seeking experiences of my life.
